docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text:
• Understand computer organization and architecture

    The distinction between organization and architecture, the Von Neumann model, the evolution of computing (Moore's law, generations), and the basic components of a computer system.

  • Master computer arithmetic

    Signed number representations, integer addition/subtraction/multiplication/division, IEEE-754 floating-point representation, and floating-point arithmetic.

  • Analyse instruction sets and CPU structure

    Instruction formats (R, I, J), addressing modes, register transfer notation, CPU register organization, and the RISC vs CISC debate.

  • Design pipelines and control units

    Pipelining stages, hazards (structural, data, control), forwarding, branch prediction, and the design of hardwired vs microprogrammed control units.

  • Design memory systems

    Cache organization (direct-mapped, set-associative, fully associative), replacement policies, write policies, AMAT analysis, virtual memory, TLB, and disk technologies.

  • Design I/O systems

    Programmed I/O, interrupt-driven I/O, DMA, bus architectures, and disk I/O performance.

  • Explore advanced topics

    Parallel processing models (SISD/SIMD/MISD/MIMD), multicore, GPU computing, low-level data structures, and an introduction to operating systems.

docs.title: Section A — Introduction and Performance (Ch 1) — 12 marks
A1. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
Computer architecture refers to:

(a) the physical implementation of the computer (b) attributes visible to a programmer (instruction set, data types, addressing) (c) the CPU clock speed (d) the operating system

docs.title: A2. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
Moore's law states that:

(a) clock speed doubles every year (b) the number of transistors per chip doubles approximately every 18–24 months (c) memory access time halves every 2 years (d) CPU power consumption doubles every decade

docs.title: A3. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
The Von Neumann bottleneck refers to:

(a) the limited number of registers (b) the transfer of instructions and data over a single bus (c) the width of the ALU (d) the cache size

docs.title: A4. Short answer [3]
docs.text: Given a program with 10⁸ instructions, an average CPI of 2.5, and a 4 GHz clock, compute: (a) the CPU execution time; (b) the MIPS rating.

docs.title: A5. Short answer [3]
docs.text: A program spends 60% of its time in a routine that can be made 3× faster. Use Amdahl's law to compute the overall speedup.

docs.title: B1. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
The decimal value of the 8-bit two's-complement number 11110110 is:

(a) −10 (b) −9 (c) −11 (d) +246

docs.title: B2. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
In IEEE-754 single precision, the exponent field is biased by:

(a) 64 (b) 127 (c) 128 (d) 255

docs.title: B3. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
Which multiplication algorithm handles signed numbers without any separate sign-handling step?

(a) shift-add (b) Booth's algorithm (c) restoring division (d) non-restoring division

docs.title: B4. Short answer [3]
docs.text: Represent the decimal number −45 in 8-bit binary as: (a) sign-magnitude; (b) 1's complement; (c) 2's complement.

docs.title: B5. Short answer [3]
docs.text: Add the 4-bit two's-complement numbers 0110 and 0101. Give the result and state whether overflow occurred. Justify your answer with a bit-level argument.

docs.title: B6. Short answer [3]
docs.text: Encode the decimal value 6.75 in IEEE-754 single precision. Show the sign bit, exponent field, mantissa field, and the final 32-bit hexadecimal value.

docs.title: Section C — Instruction Sets and CPU Structure (Ch 3) — 15 marks
C1. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
Which addressing mode computes the effective address as base register + constant offset?

(a) immediate (b) direct (c) indexed / base+offset (d) register indirect

docs.title: C2. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
In MIPS, an R-type instruction includes fields:

(a) opcode, address (b) opcode, rs, rt, immediate (c) opcode, rs, rt, rd, shamt, funct (d) opcode, target address

docs.title: C3. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
A RISC architecture is characterized by:

(a) variable-length instructions and microcode (b) fixed-length instructions, load-store architecture, many registers (c) complex addressing modes (d) microcoded instruction execution

docs.title: C4. Short answer [4]
docs.text: Decode the following MIPS machine instruction (hex): 0x012A4020. Identify the format, the operation, the source and destination registers, and write the equivalent assembly.

docs.title: C5. Short answer [3]
docs.text:
Compare the number of memory accesses required for each of the following addressing modes to fetch a single operand from a register-based datapath:

  • immediate
  • register
  • register indirect
  • direct
  • indirect

Give the effective address formula for each.

docs.title: C6. Short answer [2]
docs.text: Explain in one sentence why the program counter and the instruction register are essential for the Von Neumann instruction cycle.

docs.title: Section D — Pipelining and Control Unit (Ch 4) — 18 marks
D1. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
The maximum ideal speedup of a k-stage pipeline is:

(a) \(k^2\) (b) \(k\) (c) \(\log_2 k\) (d) \(2k\)

docs.title: D2. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
A structural hazard in a pipeline occurs when:

(a) two instructions want the same hardware resource (b) an instruction depends on the result of a previous instruction (c) a branch is taken (d) a page fault occurs

docs.title: D3. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
Branch prediction is used to address:

(a) structural hazards (b) data hazards (c) control hazards (d) cache misses

docs.title: D4. Short answer [4]
docs.text:
Consider the instruction sequence: 

ADD  R1, R2, R3
SUB  R4, R1, R5
AND  R6, R1, R7
Identify all data hazards. For each hazard, state: (a) the type of hazard (RAW, WAR, WAW); (b) the number of stall cycles needed without forwarding; (c) how forwarding resolves it (or whether a stall is still needed).

docs.title: D5. Short answer [4]
docs.text: Describe the difference between a hardwired and a microprogrammed control unit in terms of: (a) implementation complexity; (b) speed; (c) flexibility; (d) which architecture class (RISC or CISC) typically uses each.

docs.title: D6. Short answer [4]
docs.text: A program has 20% branch instructions. In a 5-stage pipeline, each taken branch causes a 2-cycle penalty. If branch prediction accuracy is 90%, compute the average CPI assuming the ideal CPI is 1.

docs.title: E1. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
The principle that justifies the memory hierarchy is:

(a) Moore's law (b) Amdahl's law (c) locality of reference (d) the Von Neumann bottleneck

docs.title: E2. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
DRAM requires periodic refresh because:

(a) it uses flip-flops (b) it stores each bit as charge on a capacitor that leaks (c) it is slower than SRAM (d) it is volatile

docs.title: E3. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
In a direct-mapped cache, the set is determined by:

(a) the tag bits (b) the block-offset bits (c) the index bits (d) the entire address

docs.title: E4. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
Write-back caching reduces memory traffic compared with write-through because:

(a) every write goes to memory (b) writes accumulate in the cache and reach memory only when the block is evicted (c) it caches only reads (d) it uses larger blocks

docs.title: E5. Short answer [4]
docs.text:
A cache has: - 32 KB total size, - 64-byte blocks, - 4-way set associativity.

Compute: (a) the number of blocks in the cache; (b) the number of sets; (c) the number of index bits; (d) the number of tag bits (for a 32-bit address); (e) the number of block-offset bits.

docs.title: E6. Short answer [4]
docs.text: A cache has a hit time of 2 ns, a miss penalty of 40 ns, and a hit rate of 95%. Compute the AMAT (average memory access time). Then compute the AMAT if the hit rate improves to 98%.

docs.title: E7. Short answer [4]
docs.text: Explain the difference between paging and segmentation. Which one suffers from internal fragmentation? Which one from external fragmentation?

docs.title: E8. Short answer [2]
docs.text: Briefly explain why an SSD has no seek time, and how this changes the relative performance of random versus sequential reads compared with an HDD.

docs.title: F1. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
In programmed I/O, the CPU:

(a) is interrupted by the device (b) transfers data using DMA (c) continuously polls the device status register (d) uses a separate I/O processor

docs.title: F2. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
DMA reduces CPU load because:

(a) the CPU is slower (b) the DMA controller transfers data between memory and device without CPU intervention (c) it uses fewer interrupts (d) it transfers whole sectors

docs.title: F3. Short answer [4]
docs.text: Compare programmed I/O, interrupt-driven I/O, and DMA on: (a) CPU involvement; (b) latency per transfer; (c) suitability for high-speed devices.

docs.title: F4. Short answer [4]
docs.text: A disk has an average seek time of 9 ms, a rotational speed of 7200 RPM, and a transfer rate of 150 MB/s. Compute: (a) the average rotational latency; (b) the average time to transfer a 4 KB block; (c) the total average service time for the transfer.

docs.title: G1. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
SIMD processing is best described as:

(a) one instruction on one datum (b) one instruction on multiple data items (c) multiple instructions on one datum (d) multiple instructions on multiple data items

docs.title: G2. Multiple choice [2]
docs.text:
A GPU achieves high throughput mainly because it:

(a) runs at a very high clock speed (b) uses thousands of simple cores to execute many threads in parallel (c) has a very large cache (d) uses faster memory than a CPU

docs.title: G3. Short answer [4]
docs.text:
For each of the following workloads, identify which architecture (SISD, SIMD, MIMD) is best suited and justify:

(a) Adding two large matrices element-wise. (b) A single-threaded text editor. (c) A web server handling 10,000 simultaneous clients. (d) A scientific simulation with loosely coupled sub-tasks.

docs.title: Grading rubric
docs.text:
Band Marks A 90–100 B 75–89 C 60–74 F < 60

Common error checks:

  • Wrong CPI or clock calculation: −2.
  • Off-by-one in addressing-mode memory-access counts: −1.
  • Confusing write-through with write-back: −2.
  • Missing overflow in 2's-complement addition: −1.
  • Wrong pipeline stall count: −2.
  • Using the wrong Amdahl's law formula: −2.
  • Confusing internal with external fragmentation: −2.
  • Treating GPU threads as CPUs: −1.

docs.title: Course description
docs.text: The course introduces the architecture and organization of a computer system and its components. Students learn how the CPU, memory, and I/O subsystems interact; how instructions are represented, decoded, and executed; and how the performance of a computer system is measured and improved. Students design and simulate a basic computer system (Logisim project).

docs.title: Course objectives and competences
docs.text:

  1. Introduce the architecture and organization of a computer system and its components.
  2. Design and simulate a basic computer system.

docs.title: Course content
docs.text:
Chapter 1 — Introduction and Performance

  • Organization vs architecture
  • Computer evolution (generations, Moore's law)
  • Von Neumann model
  • Basic computer components (CPU, memory, I/O, buses)
  • Instruction cycle (fetch-decode-execute)
  • Performance metrics: clock rate, CPI, MIPS, FLOPS
  • The performance equation
  • Amdahl's law
  • Benchmarks (SPEC, Geekbench)

Chapter 2 — Computer Arithmetic

  • Number representation: sign-magnitude, 1's complement, 2's complement, biased
  • Integer addition and subtraction
  • Overflow detection
  • Multiplication: shift-add, Booth's algorithm
  • Division: restoring, non-restoring
  • Floating-point representation: IEEE 754 (single, double, extended)
  • Floating-point arithmetic (addition, multiplication)
  • Rounding and exceptions

Chapter 3 — Instruction Sets and CPU Structure

  • Instruction set taxonomy (stack, accumulator, general-purpose)
  • Instruction formats (R, I, J)
  • Addressing modes (immediate, direct, indirect, register, register indirect, indexed, base+offset, relative)
  • Operand types and operations
  • CPU register organization (PC, IR, MAR, MBR, AC, general-purpose)
  • Register transfer notation (RTN)
  • Datapath design
  • RISC vs CISC

Chapter 4 — Pipelining and Control Unit

  • Pipeline concept and speedup

docs.title: Chapter 1 — Introduction and Performance
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Contact hours: 2 lecture + 3 tutorial/lab · Home study: ~5 h

Coverage: organization vs architecture · computer evolution · the Von Neumann model · components of a computer system · instruction cycle · performance metrics · Amdahl's law · benchmarks.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
1. Distinguish computer architecture from computer organization and give examples of each.
  2. Trace the evolution of computing through its generations and Moore's law.
  3. Describe the Von Neumann model and identify the role of each subsystem.
  4. Trace the instruction cycle (fetch, decode, execute).
  5. Compute the CPU performance equation and apply Amdahl's law to evaluate a proposed optimisation.

docs.title: 1.1 Organization vs. architecture
docs.text:
Definition (Stallings §1.1)

Computer architecture refers to those attributes of a system visible to a programmer — the instruction set, data types, addressing modes, and I/O mechanisms. Computer organization refers to the operational units and their interconnections that realize the architectural specification — control signals, memory technology, and interfaces.

The distinction is analogous to the distinction between the specification of a programming language and the implementation of its compiler:

Aspect Architecture Organization Visible to programmer Yes No Example Whether an instruction MUL exists Whether MUL is implemented by a hardware multiplier or by repeated addition Example Word size (32 or 64 bits) The technology of the memory (SRAM vs DRAM) Example Number of registers The physical wiring of the register file

Why the distinction matters

Two CPUs can be architecturally identical but organizationally different — same instruction set, different implementation. This is why Intel and AMD x86 CPUs run the same binaries but have very different microarchitectures, power envelopes, and performance profiles.

docs.title: 1.2.1 The generations
docs.text: Generation Era Technology Characteristics First 1945–1955 Vacuum tubes ENIAC; 5,000 additions/second Second 1955–1965 Transistors IBM 7094, smaller and more reliable Third 1965–1980 Integrated circuits IBM System/360, DEC PDP-11 Fourth 1980–present VLSI PCs, mobile, servers

docs.title: 1.2.2 Moore's law
docs.text:
Moore's law

The number of transistors on a chip doubles approximately every 18–24 months, while the cost per transistor falls proportionally.

Moore's law drove a 40-year exponential in computing capability. It has slowed since ~2010 because:

  • Power density (Dennard scaling) broke down.
  • Manufacturing costs rise at advanced nodes (7 nm, 5 nm, 3 nm).
  • Physical limits (transistor size, wire delay) loom.

The industry's response has shifted from higher clock speed to more parallelism — multicore CPUs, GPUs, and specialised accelerators.

docs.title: 1.2.3 The Von Neumann bottleneck
docs.text:
In a Von Neumann machine, both instructions and data share the same memory and the same bus between CPU and memory. The processor therefore cannot fetch an instruction and a data word in the same cycle — a bandwidth limit known as the Von Neumann bottleneck.

The Harvard architecture separates instruction and data memories, doubling the effective bandwidth. Modern CPUs use modified Harvard designs — separate L1 instruction and data caches, but a unified L2/L3 hierarchy.

docs.title: 1.3 The Von Neumann model
docs.text:
┌─────────────┐         ┌──────────────┐
│             │◄───────►│              │
│    CPU      │  Bus    │    Memory    │
│             │◄───────►│              │
└─────┬───────┘         └──────────────┘
      │
      │
┌─────▼───────┐
│  I/O        │
│  Devices    │
└─────────────┘

The Von Neumann model has four components:

  1. CPU — executes instructions. Contains the ALU (arithmetic-logic unit), the control unit, and registers.
  2. Memory — stores both instructions and data, addressed by location.
  3. I/O — interacts with the outside world.
  4. Bus — carries addresses, data, and control signals between the components.

docs.title: 1.4 The instruction cycle
docs.text:
Every instruction goes through three phases (sometimes split into more):

Fetch  →  Decode  →  Execute

Fetch: 1. CPU puts the PC value on the address bus. 2. Memory returns the instruction at that address. 3. CPU loads the instruction into the IR and increments the PC.

Decode: 1. Control unit reads the opcode and determines the instruction type. 2. Source operands are read from the register file.

Execute: 1. ALU performs the operation (or memory access, or branch). 2. Result is written back to a register (or memory).

Many architectures add memory and write-back stages, yielding a five-stage pipeline (Chapter 4).

docs.title: 1.5.1 Clock rate and cycle time
docs.text: The clock rate \(f\) (Hz) determines how many cycles per second the CPU executes. The cycle time is \(\tau = 1/f\).

docs.title: 1.5.2 The performance equation
docs.text:
CPU time formula (Patterson & Hennessy)

\[\text{CPU time} = \text{IC} \times \text{CPI} \times \tau = \frac{\text{IC} \times \text{CPI}}{f}\]

where: - \(\text{IC}\) = instruction count (total instructions executed); - \(\text{CPI}\) = cycles per instruction (average); - \(\tau\) = clock period; \(f\) = clock rate.

The three factors are interdependent. Reducing IC (fewer, more powerful instructions) usually raises CPI. Increasing \(f\) often increases CPI because pipeline stages become harder to balance.

docs.title: 1.5.3 MIPS and FLOPS
docs.text:
MIPS (millions of instructions per second):

\[ \text{MIPS} = \frac{\text{IC}}{T \times 10^6} = \frac{f}{\text{CPI} \times 10^6} \]

MIPS is misleading — it ignores the complexity of instructions. A CISC machine can have higher MIPS than a RISC machine but lower throughput.

FLOPS (floating-point operations per second) is more meaningful for scientific workloads.

docs.title: 1.5.4 Amdahl's law
docs.text:
Amdahl's law

If a fraction \(f\) of the execution time is improved by a factor \(s\), the overall speedup is

\[S = \frac{1}{(1 - f) + f/s}\]

The speedup is bounded by \(1/(1-f)\) as \(s \to \infty\).

Implication. An optimisation that only improves \(10\%\) of the code can give at most a \(1/(1-0.1) \approx 1.11\) speedup — no matter how fast the improved part becomes. Amdahl's law is the fundamental argument for parallel computing: as serial fractions approach zero, the potential speedup approaches the processor count.

docs.title: Worked example 1.1 — CPU performance
docs.text:
Given. - IC = \(10^8\) instructions. - CPI = 2.5. - Clock = 4 GHz.

CPU time:

\[ T = \frac{10^8 \times 2.5}{4 \times 10^9} = 0.0625\,\text{s} = 62.5\,\text{ms}. \]

MIPS:

\[ \text{MIPS} = \frac{4 \times 10^9}{2.5 \times 10^6} = 1600\,\text{MIPS}. \]

docs.title: Worked example 1.2 — Amdahl's law
docs.text:
Given. A program spends 60% of its time in a routine made 3× faster.

Speedup:

\[ S = \frac{1}{(1 - 0.6) + 0.6/3} = \frac{1}{0.4 + 0.2} = \frac{1}{0.6} \approx 1.67. \]

The maximum possible speedup even if the routine became infinitely fast is:

\[ S_{\max} = \frac{1}{1 - 0.6} = 2.5. \]

So even a perfect optimisation of that routine yields at most a 2.5× speedup.

docs.title: 1.5.5 Benchmarks
docs.text:
Real workloads vary enormously. To compare systems fairly, industry uses standard benchmark suites:

  • SPEC CPU — integer and floating-point benchmarks.
  • SPECpower — energy efficiency.
  • Geekbench — mobile and desktop.
  • STREAM — memory bandwidth.
  • Linpack — floating-point (basis of the TOP500 supercomputer ranking).

Benchmarks are not perfect — vendors can "optimise for the benchmark" — but they are the least-bad way to compare systems.

docs.title: 1.6 Quiz
docs.text:
1. Distinguish computer architecture from computer organization. Give two examples of each.
  2. State Moore's law. Why has it slowed since ~2010?
  3. Describe the instruction cycle. What is stored in the PC and IR?
  4. Compute the CPU time for a program with IC = \(5 \times 10^8\), CPI = 1.8, clock = 3 GHz.
  5. A program spends 40% of its time in a loop that can be made 2× faster. Use Amdahl's law to compute the speedup.

docs.title: Answer key
docs.text:
Click to reveal
  1. Architecture: visible to programmer — instruction set, word size. Organization: implementation — SRAM vs DRAM, pipeline depth.
  2. Transistor count doubles every 18–24 months. Slowed because power density, manufacturing costs, and physical limits have caught up with the doubling.
  3. Fetch (PC → IR, PC increment), decode (opcode), execute (ALU/memory). PC holds the address of the next instruction; IR holds the current instruction.
  4. \(T = (5 \times 10^8 \times 1.8) / (3 \times 10^9) = 0.3\,\text{s}\).
  5. \(S = 1/(0.6 + 0.4/2) = 1/0.8 = 1.25\).

docs.text:
• Stallings, §1.1–§2.5.
  • Mano, §1.1–§1.3.
  • Patterson & Hennessy, §1.1–§1.9.

docs.title: Chapter 2 — Computer Arithmetic
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Contact hours: 2 lecture + 3 tutorial/lab · Home study: ~5 h

Coverage: signed number representation · integer addition and subtraction · overflow detection · multiplication (shift-add, Booth) · division (restoring, non-restoring) · IEEE-754 floating point · floating-point arithmetic · rounding.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
1. Convert between sign-magnitude, 1's complement, 2's complement, and biased representations.
  2. Perform integer addition and subtraction and detect overflow at the bit level.
  3. Trace Booth's multiplication algorithm on a small example.
  4. Trace restoring and non-restoring division on a small example.
  5. Encode and decode IEEE-754 single and double precision values.
  6. Perform floating-point addition and identify rounding sources.

docs.title: 2.1.1 Sign-magnitude
docs.text:
The most-significant bit is the sign (\(0\) for positive, \(1\) for negative); the rest is the magnitude.

Problem: two representations of zero (0000 and 1000), and addition requires sign handling.

docs.title: 2.1.2 1's complement
docs.text:
Negative numbers are the bitwise complement of their positive counterpart.

Still two zeros — 0000 (positive) and 1111 (negative) — and end-around carry in addition.

docs.title: 2.1.3 2's complement
docs.text:
2's complement (dominant today)

To negate a number, complement all bits and add 1.

Properties:

  • One zero.
  • Addition and subtraction use the same circuit.
  • Range for \(n\) bits: \(-2^{n-1}\) to \(2^{n-1} - 1\).

docs.title: 2.1.4 Biased (offset) representation
docs.text: Add a bias \(B\) to the true value: stored = \(x + B\). Used in floating-point exponents (IEEE 754 uses bias \(127\) for single precision).

docs.title: Worked example 2.1 — −45 in 8 bits
docs.text: Representation Bits Sign-magnitude 1_0101101 1's complement 11010010 2's complement 11010011 Biased (B=127) \(127 - 45 = 82\) = 01010010

docs.title: 2.2.1 2's-complement addition
docs.text: Add the bits as unsigned, discard the carry out of the MSB, and interpret the result as 2's-complement.

docs.title: 2.2.2 Overflow detection
docs.text:
Overflow occurs when the true mathematical result is outside the representable range.

The sign rule for 2's-complement addition

Overflow occurs if and only if: - Both operands are positive and the result is negative, OR - Both operands are negative and the result is positive.

Formally: \(C_{\text{in}} \oplus C_{\text{out}}\) of the MSB.

docs.title: Worked example 2.2 — overflow detection
docs.text:
Add 0110 (+6) and 0101 (+5) in 4-bit 2's complement:

  0110
+ 0101
------
  1011   (result = -5)

Both operands are positive, result is negative → overflow.

The correct mathematical answer is 11, which cannot be represented in 4-bit 2's complement (max = +7).

docs.title: 2.3.1 Shift-add (unsigned)
docs.text:
For two \(n\)-bit unsigned numbers:

product = 0
for i in 0..n-1:
    if multiplier[i] == 1:
        product += multiplicand << i

Takes \(n\) cycles (or fewer with a multiplier array).

docs.title: 2.3.2 Booth's algorithm (signed)
docs.text:
Booth's algorithm handles signed multiplication uniformly. It examines the current and previous multiplier bits:

\((Q_i, Q_{i-1})\) Action 0 0 No arithmetic 0 1 Add multiplicand 1 0 Subtract multiplicand 1 1 No arithmetic

docs.title: Worked example 2.3 — Booth's algorithm
docs.text:
Multiply \(+3\) (multiplicand) by \(-2\) (multiplier), both in 4-bit 2's complement:

  • Multiplicand \(M = 0011\) (+3), \(-M = 1101\).
  • Multiplier \(Q = 1110\) (−2), \(Q_{-1} = 0\).
Step \(Q_0 Q_{-1}\) Operation \(A\) \(Q\) 0 — initialise 0000 1110 · 0 1 1 0 \(A \leftarrow A - M = 1101\); arith shift right 1110 1111 · 0 2 1 0 \(A \leftarrow A - M = 1011\); arith shift right 1101 1111 · 1 3 1 1 no op; arith shift right 1110 1111 · 1 4 1 1 no op; arith shift right 1111 1111 · 1

Result: \(AQ = 1111\,1111_{2}\) = \(−1\) = \((+3) \times (−2)\). ✓

docs.title: 2.4.1 Restoring division
docs.text:
1. Shift left \(A\) (partial remainder).
  2. Subtract divisor from \(A\).
  3. If \(A < 0\): restore (add divisor back), set \(Q_0 = 0\).
  4. Else: set \(Q_0 = 1\).
  5. Repeat \(n\) times.

docs.title: 2.4.2 Non-restoring division
docs.text:
Avoids the restore step by alternating between subtraction and addition:

  • If \(A \geq 0\): \(A \leftarrow 2A - M\).
  • If \(A < 0\): \(A \leftarrow 2A + M\).

At the end, a final restore is done only if \(A\) is negative.

Non-restoring division is faster (no restore each iteration) but requires careful sign tracking.

docs.title: 2.5.1 Format
docs.text:
IEEE 754 single precision is 32 bits:

| S | EEEEEEEE | MMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMM |
 1    8               23
  • S = sign bit.
  • E = biased exponent (bias 127 for single).
  • M = mantissa (fractional part).

The value is

\[ (-1)^S \times 1.M \times 2^{E - 127} \]

where \(1.M\) is the hidden leading bit convention.

Double precision: 64 bits = 1 sign + 11 exponent (bias 1023) + 52 mantissa.

docs.title: 2.5.2 Special values
docs.text: Exponent Mantissa Meaning 0 0 \(\pm 0\) 0 \(\neq 0\) Subnormal numbers 1–254 any Normal numbers 255 0 \(\pm \infty\) 255 \(\neq 0\) NaN

docs.title: 2.5.3 Floating-point arithmetic
docs.text:
Addition requires alignment: the exponent with the smaller value is shifted right until the exponents match, then the mantissas are added.

Multiplication multiplies the mantissas and adds the exponents.

Rounding modes (IEEE 754):

  • round to nearest, ties to even (default);
  • round toward zero;
  • round toward \(+\infty\);
  • round toward \(-\infty\).

docs.title: 2.5.4 Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Floating-point addition is not associative: (a+b)+c may differ from a+(b+c).
  • Comparisons with == are dangerous — use a tolerance.
  • Subtracting nearly-equal numbers can cause catastrophic cancellation.
  • Accumulated sums can drift; Kahan summation mitigates this.

docs.title: 2.6 Quiz
docs.text:
1. Represent −45 in 8-bit sign-magnitude, 1's complement, and 2's complement.
  2. Add 0110 and 0101 in 4-bit 2's complement. Did overflow occur? Why?
  3. Explain how Booth's algorithm handles negative multipliers without a separate sign step.
  4. Encode 6.75 in IEEE-754 single precision.
  5. Add \(1.5 \times 10^{38}\) and \(-1.5 \times 10^{38}\) (both single precision, both normal). What is the result, and what happens if you then add \(1.0\)?

docs.title: Answer key
docs.text:
Click to reveal
  1. Sign-magnitude 10101101, 1's complement 11010010, 2's complement 11010011.
  2. Result 1011 = −5; overflow because both inputs are positive but result is negative.
  3. Booth's algorithm examines adjacent multiplier bits and performs add/subtract/skip accordingly — the sign of the multiplier is naturally handled.
  4. 0x40D80000 (see worked example).
  5. Result 0. Adding 1.0 to 0 gives 1.0; the original precision of the operands is lost — an example of catastrophic cancellation.

docs.title: Chapter 3 — Instruction Sets and CPU Structure
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Contact hours: 2 lecture + 3 tutorial/lab · Home study: ~5 h

Coverage: instruction set taxonomy · instruction formats · addressing modes · operand types and operations · CPU registers and datapath · register transfer notation · RISC vs CISC.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
1. Classify instruction sets by operand source (stack, accumulator, general-purpose).
  2. Decode R, I, and J instruction formats.
  3. Compute effective addresses for the eight classic addressing modes.
  4. Write register transfer notation (RTN) for a simple datapath.
  5. Compare RISC and CISC on code size, CPI, pipeline depth, and compiler complexity.

docs.title: 3.1 Instruction set taxonomy
docs.text:
Instruction sets differ in where the operands come from:

Class Operand source Stack effect Example Stack Top of a pushdown stack Push/pop Old HP calculators, Java bytecode Accumulator A single accumulator Implicit Early 8-bit CPUs General-purpose Many registers Explicit MIPS, x86, ARM Register-memory One operand in memory Explicit x86 Load-store All operands in registers; separate load/store Explicit MIPS, ARM, RISC-V

The load-store model is the foundation of RISC (Section 3.6).

docs.title: 3.2.1 MIPS R-type (register-to-register)
docs.text:
| opcode 6 | rs 5 | rt 5 | rd 5 | shamt 5 | funct 6 |

Example: add rd, rs, rt → 000000 rs rt rd 00000 100000.

docs.title: 3.2.2 MIPS I-type (immediate)
docs.text:
| opcode 6 | rs 5 | rt 5 | immediate 16 |

Example: addi rt, rs, imm16.

docs.title: 3.2.3 MIPS J-type (jump)
docs.text:
| opcode 6 | target address 26 |

Target = (PC+4)[31:28] || target << 2.

docs.title: Worked example 3.1 — decode 0x012A4020
docs.text:
Binary: 0000 0001 0010 1010 0100 0000 0010 0000

Break into fields:

  • opcode = 000000 → R-type.
  • rs = 01001 = 9.
  • rt = 01010 = 10.
  • rd = 01000 = 8.
  • shamt = 00000.
  • funct = 100000 = 0x20 = add.

Decoded: add $8, $9, $10.

docs.title: 3.3 Addressing modes
docs.text:
Mode Effective address (EA) Memory accesses Immediate operand is in instruction 0 Register operand is in register 0 Direct EA = address field 1 Indirect EA = M[address field] 2 Register indirect EA = R[field] 1 Displacement (base+offset) EA = R[base] + offset 1 Indexed EA = R[index] + address field 1 Relative EA = PC + offset 1

The base+offset mode is the workhorse of modern ISAs — it supports array indexing, structure field access, and stack frame access with a single encoding.

docs.title: 3.4 CPU registers
docs.text:
A general-purpose CPU has these registers:

Register Purpose PC Program counter — address of the next instruction IR Instruction register — current instruction MAR Memory address register MBR / MDR Memory buffer / data register AC Accumulator (in accumulator ISAs) R0..Rn General-purpose registers SP Stack pointer FLAGS / PSW Condition codes (zero, carry, sign, overflow)

docs.title: 3.4.1 Register transfer notation
docs.text:
RTN describes data movement and operations:

MAR ← PC
M[MAR] → MBR
IR ← MBR
PC ← PC + 4

Each line executes in one cycle (or a small number of cycles depending on the datapath).

docs.title: Worked example 3.2 — fetch cycle in RTN
docs.text:
T0: MAR ← PC
T1: MBR ← M[MAR], PC ← PC + 4
T2: IR  ← MBR

Three cycles, assuming a single-bus datapath where each transfer takes one cycle.

docs.title: 3.5 Datapath
docs.text:
The datapath is the collection of registers, ALU, and internal buses that carry out the operations.

A single-cycle datapath executes one instruction per cycle. Fetch, decode, execute, memory, and write-back all happen in the same cycle — the clock must be long enough for the slowest path.

A multi-cycle datapath breaks the instruction into 3–5 phases, each taking one cycle. This allows a shorter clock period but adds control complexity.

A pipelined datapath overlaps the phases of multiple instructions (Chapter 4).

docs.title: 3.6 RISC vs CISC
docs.text:
Feature RISC CISC Instruction length Fixed Variable Instruction count Simple, few Complex, many Operands Registers only (load-store) Registers or memory Registers Many (32+) Few (8–16) Addressing modes Few Many Control Hardwired Microprogrammed CPI Near 1 Higher (2–10) Code size Larger Smaller Pipelining Easy Hard Examples MIPS, ARM, RISC-V x86

The RISC argument (Patterson & Hennessy, 1980s). Most CISC instructions were rarely used; compilers could generate efficient code from a small RISC subset; simple instructions pipeline better; register-only operands are faster.

The modern synthesis. Modern x86 (Intel Core, AMD Zen) internally decodes CISC instructions into RISC-like micro-operations — so today's distinction is largely about the external ISA, not the internal microarchitecture.

docs.title: 3.7 Quiz
docs.text:
1. Classify the MIPS instruction set (stack, accumulator, or general-purpose load-store).
  2. Decode 0x012A4020.
  3. Give the effective address for lw $t0, 8($sp).
  4. Write RTN for add $1, $2, $3.
  5. Compare RISC and CISC on pipeline depth and code size.

docs.title: Answer key
docs.text:
Click to reveal
  1. Load-store general-purpose.
  2. add $8, $9, $10.
  3. EA = R[sp] + 8.
  4. R[1] ← R[2] + R[3].
  5. RISC: shorter pipeline, larger code; CISC: longer pipeline, smaller code.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Stallings, §12.1–§13.3.
  • Mano, §5.1–§7.4.
  • Patterson & Hennessy, §2.1–§2.9.

docs.title: Chapter 4 — Pipelining and Control Unit
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Coverage: pipeline concept and speedup · five-stage RISC pipeline · hazards · forwarding and stalling · branch prediction · hardwired and microprogrammed control.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
1. Compute pipeline speedup under ideal and realistic conditions.
  2. Identify structural, data, and control hazards in an instruction sequence.
  3. Apply forwarding and stalling to resolve data hazards.
  4. Evaluate branch prediction schemes.
  5. Design a hardwired control unit for a simple ISA.

docs.title: 4.1 Pipeline concept
docs.text:
A pipeline overlaps the execution of multiple instructions by breaking each into stages. If each stage takes \(\tau\) and there are \(k\) stages, the first instruction takes \(k\tau\); thereafter, one completes per cycle.

Ideal speedup: \(S = k\).

Realistic speedup: limited by hazards, pipeline fill/drain, and imbalanced stage lengths.

docs.title: 4.1.1 Five-stage RISC pipeline
docs.text:
Stage Purpose IF Fetch instruction from memory ID Decode, read registers EX ALU operation or address calculation MEM Read/write data memory WB Write result to register

Total cycle time = max stage time + register overhead.

docs.title: 4.2.1 Structural hazards
docs.text: Two instructions want the same hardware in the same cycle (e.g., IF and MEM both need memory in a single-memory design). Solved by separate instruction/data memories (Harvard) or by stalling.

docs.title: 4.2.2 Data hazards
docs.text:
An instruction needs a value that a previous instruction has not yet produced. Three types:

  • RAW (read-after-write): the real one — always present.
  • WAR (write-after-read): anti-dependence, eliminated by register renaming.
  • WAW (write-after-write): output dependence, eliminated by renaming.

Forwarding (bypass) routes the ALU output directly to the input of a later instruction, avoiding the WB stage.

Load-use hazard cannot be resolved by forwarding — the value is only available after MEM. One stall cycle is required.

docs.title: 4.2.3 Control hazards
docs.text:
Caused by branches: the pipeline fetches the wrong instructions until the branch is resolved. Solutions:

  • Stall until branch resolution (costly).
  • Predict not-taken (cheap, wrong for taken branches).
  • Delayed branch — execute one instruction from the delay slot.
  • Branch prediction — static (compile-time) or dynamic (runtime, using branch history tables).

docs.title: Worked example 4.1 — detecting hazards
docs.text:
Sequence: 

ADD  R1, R2, R3      (produces R1)
SUB  R4, R1, R5      (uses R1)  ← RAW
AND  R6, R1, R7      (uses R1)  ← RAW

Without forwarding: SUB stalls 2 cycles, AND stalls 2 cycles → 4 stall cycles.

With forwarding: - SUB gets R1 from ALU output → 1-cycle stall. - AND can read the value from the forwarding path after the ADD's EX stage → no stall (its EX happens in cycle 6, ADD's result available in cycle 4).

Result: 1 stall cycle.

docs.title: Worked example 4.2 — branch penalty
docs.text:
Given: - 20% branches. - 2-cycle penalty for taken branches (in a 5-stage pipeline). - Branch prediction accuracy 90%. - Ideal CPI = 1.

Average CPI:

\[ \text{CPI} = 1 + (0.20 \times 0.10 \times 2) = 1 + 0.04 = 1.04. \]

Misprediction penalty applies only to 10% of 20% = 2% of instructions, each costing 2 cycles.

docs.title: 4.3.1 Hardwired control
docs.text:
The control unit is a finite-state machine — combinational logic generating control signals from the opcode and state.

Pros: Fast (single-cycle decode), efficient for small, regular ISAs. Cons: Difficult to modify — adding an instruction requires redesign. Used by: RISC architectures (MIPS, RISC-V).

docs.title: 4.3.2 Microprogrammed control
docs.text:
The control unit is a microprogram stored in control memory. Each machine instruction is a sequence of microinstructions that assert the appropriate control signals.

Pros: Flexible, easy to add instructions (add microcode), good for complex ISAs. Cons: Slower (each instruction requires multiple microinstruction fetches). Used by: CISC architectures (classic x86, VAX).

docs.title: 4.3.3 Wilkes' control unit model
docs.text:
Maurice Wilkes (1951) proposed that the control unit is a microprogram executed by a micro-sequencer:

Control Memory (microcode)
        ↓
  Microinstruction Register
        ↓
  Micro-sequencer (next-address logic)
        ↓
  Control signals to datapath

Horizontal microcode uses one bit per control line — wide instructions but parallel. Vertical microcode uses a compact encoding — narrow instructions but needs a decoder.

docs.title: 4.4 Quiz
docs.text:
1. What is the ideal speedup of a 5-stage pipeline? What limits the actual speedup?
  2. Identify the hazard type in each of these pairs: (a) ADD R1,R2,R3 then SUB R4,R1,R5; (b) LW R1,0(R2) then ADD R3,R1,R4.
  3. Why can't forwarding resolve a load-use hazard?
  4. Explain the difference between horizontal and vertical microcode.
  5. Compute the average CPI given: ideal CPI = 1, 25% branches, prediction accuracy 85%, taken-branch penalty 3 cycles.

docs.title: Answer key
docs.text:
Click to reveal
  1. Ideal \(= 5\). Limited by hazards, fill/drain, and stage imbalance.
  2. (a) RAW, (b) RAW (load-use).
  3. The value only appears after the MEM stage; the next instruction's EX stage starts before the load's value is available.
  4. Horizontal: one bit per control signal, wide but parallel. Vertical: encoded, narrow but needs decoding.
  5. \(\text{CPI} = 1 + 0.25 \times 0.15 \times 3 = 1.1125\).

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Stallings, §14.1–§14.5, §17.1–§17.4.
  • Patterson & Hennessy, §4.1–§4.8.

docs.title: Chapter 5 — Memory Systems
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Coverage: memory hierarchy · SRAM, DRAM, ROM, flash · main memory organization · cache organization · replacement and write policies · AMAT · virtual memory · TLB · HDD and SSD.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
1. Explain the memory hierarchy and the principle of locality of reference.
  2. Compare SRAM, DRAM, ROM, and flash on speed, cost, and volatility.
  3. Design a cache (direct-mapped, set-associative, fully associative) and compute AMAT.
  4. Describe virtual memory and the role of the TLB.
  5. Compare HDD and SSD on latency and throughput.

docs.title: 5.1 Memory hierarchy
docs.text:
Memory is organised as a hierarchy — smaller and faster technologies at the top, larger and slower at the bottom:

Registers          (< 1 KB, < 1 ns)
    ↓
L1 Cache           (32 KB, ~1 ns)
    ↓
L2 Cache           (256 KB, ~5 ns)
    ↓
L3 Cache           (8 MB, ~20 ns)
    ↓
Main Memory (DRAM) (8 GB, ~80 ns)
    ↓
SSD                (256 GB, ~100 µs)
    ↓
HDD                (4 TB, ~10 ms)

The hierarchy works because of locality of reference:

  • Temporal locality — recently used items are likely to be used again.
  • Spatial locality — items near recently used items are likely to be used soon.

docs.title: 5.2 Memory technologies
docs.text:
Type Volatile? Speed Cost Typical use SRAM Yes Fastest Expensive Cache DRAM Yes Medium Cheap Main memory ROM No Slow Cheap Firmware Flash No Medium Cheap SSD, USB HDD No Very slow Very cheap Bulk storage

DRAM refresh: each cell stores a bit as charge on a capacitor. Charge leaks, so each row must be refreshed every 64 ms. SRAM uses flip-flops — no refresh needed.

docs.title: 5.3 Main memory organization
docs.text:
Memory is addressed by word or by byte. Access can be:

  • Word-at-a-time — one word per access.
  • Interleaved — multiple memory banks accessed in parallel, effectively multiplying bandwidth.

Interleaving with \(k\) banks allows \(k\) concurrent accesses, one per bank, amortising latency.

docs.title: 5.4 Cache organization
docs.text: The three classic cache organisations differ in where a given memory block may be placed:

docs.title: 5.4.1 Direct-mapped
docs.text:
Each block has exactly one allowed cache line: \(\text{line} = \text{block}\bmod N\).

Pros: simple, fast (one comparator). Cons: conflict misses (two blocks mapping to the same line thrash).

docs.title: 5.4.2 Fully associative
docs.text:
Any block can go anywhere.

Pros: no conflict misses. Cons: requires comparing the tag against every line — expensive.

docs.title: 5.4.3 Set-associative
docs.text:
A compromise: the cache has \(S\) sets, each with \(K\) ways. A block goes to one set, but within the set any way.

Typical values: 2-, 4-, 8-way set associative. Modern L1 caches are usually 4- or 8-way.

docs.title: 5.4.4 Address decomposition
docs.text:
For a set-associative cache, the address splits into:

| Tag | Index | Block offset |
  • Block offset bits: \(\log_2(\text{block size})\).
  • Index bits: \(\log_2(\text{number of sets})\).
  • Tag bits: remaining bits.

docs.title: Worked example 5.1 — cache parameters
docs.text:
Given: 32 KB cache, 64-byte blocks, 4-way set associative, 32-bit address.

  • Blocks = \(32\text{ KB} / 64\text{ B} = 512\).
  • Sets = \(512 / 4 = 128\).
  • Index bits = \(\log_2 128 = 7\).
  • Block offset bits = \(\log_2 64 = 6\).
  • Tag bits = \(32 - 7 - 6 = 19\).

docs.title: 5.5.1 Replacement policies
docs.text:
Policy Description LRU Evict the least-recently used line FIFO Evict the oldest line Random Evict a random line Optimal Evict the line used furthest in the future (theoretical)

LRU is best but expensive to implement for high associativity. Practical caches use approximations (pseudo-LRU, or random for high associativity).

docs.title: 5.5.2 Write policies
docs.text:
• Write-through — write both cache and memory on every write. Simple, but heavy traffic.
  • Write-back — write to cache only; memory is updated when the line is evicted (dirty line). Less traffic, but requires a dirty bit and complicates coherence in multicore systems.

docs.title: 5.6 AMAT — average memory access time
docs.text:
AMAT formula

\[\text{AMAT} = \text{Hit time} + \text{Miss rate} \times \text{Miss penalty}\]

Worked example 5.2 — AMAT

Given: Hit time = 2 ns, miss penalty = 40 ns, hit rate 95%.

\[ \text{AMAT} = 2 + 0.05 \times 40 = 2 + 2 = 4\,\text{ns}. \]

With hit rate 98%:

\[ \text{AMAT} = 2 + 0.02 \times 40 = 2 + 0.8 = 2.8\,\text{ns}. \]

A 3% improvement in hit rate reduces AMAT by 30% — cache hit rate is critical.

docs.title: 5.7 Virtual memory
docs.text:
Virtual memory

Virtual memory gives each process its own address space, mapped by hardware (the MMU) to physical memory. Blocks (pages) not resident in physical memory are fetched from disk on demand.

docs.title: 5.7.1 Paging vs. segmentation
docs.text:
• Paging — fixed-size pages and frames. No external fragmentation; internal fragmentation on the last page of a process.
  • Segmentation — variable-size logical segments. No internal fragmentation; external fragmentation of physical memory.

docs.title: 5.7.2 The TLB
docs.text:
The translation lookaside buffer (TLB) caches recent page-table entries. On a TLB hit, translation is fast; on a miss, the page table is consulted (possibly multiple levels).

Effective access time:

\[ \text{EAT} = \alpha (t_{\text{TLB}} + t_{\text{mem}}) + (1-\alpha)(t_{\text{TLB}} + 2 t_{\text{mem}}) \]

where \(\alpha\) is the hit ratio. With \(\alpha\) near 99%, virtual memory is effectively free.

docs.title: 5.8.1 HDD (hard disk drive)
docs.text:
• Rotating platters, read/write heads, tracks, sectors.
  • Seek time (~5–10 ms) — move the head.
  • Rotational latency (~4 ms at 7200 RPM) — wait for the sector.
  • Transfer time — read the block.

Random I/O is dominated by seek + rotation, so HDD performance for random small reads is ~100–200 IOPS.

docs.title: 5.8.2 SSD (solid-state drive)
docs.text:
• NAND flash, no moving parts.
  • No seek time — random access is ~100 µs, sequential is ~50 µs.
  • Wear-leveling — flash cells wear out after ~10⁴–10⁵ erases.
  • Write amplification — a small write may trigger a larger internal write.

Modern systems use SSDs for the primary store and HDDs (or cloud object storage) for bulk/backup.

docs.title: 5.9 Quiz
docs.text:
1. Explain the principle of locality and its two forms.
  2. Why does DRAM need refresh? Why does SRAM not?
  3. Compute the number of tag bits for a 32-bit address in a 64 KB, 4-way set-associative cache with 32-byte blocks.
  4. Compute AMAT for a cache with hit time 1 ns, miss penalty 20 ns, and hit rate 97%.
  5. Compare HDD and SSD for random-read workloads.

docs.title: Answer key
docs.text:
Click to reveal
  1. Temporal (reuse of recent items), spatial (reuse of nearby items).
  2. DRAM stores charge on a capacitor that leaks; SRAM uses flip-flops, no leakage.
  3. Blocks = 64KB/32 = 2048; sets = 2048/4 = 512; index = 9; offset = 5; tag = 32-9-5 = 18.
  4. AMAT = 1 + 0.03 × 20 = 1.6 ns.
  5. SSD has no seek/rotation, so random reads are ~100× faster than HDD.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Stallings, §4.1–§4.5, §5.1–§5.4, §6.1–§6.6.
  • Patterson & Hennessy, §5.1–§5.8.

docs.title: Chapter 6 — I/O Systems
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Coverage: I/O devices · I/O modules · programmed I/O · interrupt-driven I/O · DMA · buses · disk I/O performance · buffering.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
1. Classify I/O devices and interfaces.
  2. Compare programmed, interrupt-driven, and DMA transfer on CPU involvement and speed.
  3. Compute disk I/O throughput for a given workload.
  4. Describe modern bus hierarchies (PCIe, USB).

docs.title: 6.1 I/O devices
docs.text: Class Examples Transfer unit Access Block HDD, SSD, USB drive Block (512 B – 4 KB) Random Character Keyboard, serial port Byte Sequential Network Ethernet, Wi-Fi Packet Streaming

docs.title: 6.2 I/O modules
docs.text:
An I/O module (or controller) sits between the bus and the device. It contains:

  • Data registers — hold the transferred data.
  • Status register — ready, busy, error.
  • Control register — start, direction.

The CPU communicates with the module via memory-mapped I/O (device registers appear at memory addresses) or isolated I/O (separate address space).

docs.title: 6.3.1 Programmed I/O (polling)
docs.text:
The CPU continuously checks the status register:

while (!(status & READY)) ;
data = device.data;

Pros: simple, no interrupts. Cons: wastes CPU cycles (100% CPU is spent polling).

docs.title: 6.3.2 Interrupt-driven I/O
docs.text:
The device raises an interrupt when ready. The CPU executes other instructions in the meantime.

Pros: efficient for slow devices (keyboard, mouse). Cons: interrupt overhead per transfer — for high-speed devices, interrupts can overwhelm the CPU.

docs.title: 6.3.3 Direct Memory Access (DMA)
docs.text:
A DMA controller transfers data directly between memory and device without CPU involvement. The CPU sets up the transfer (source, destination, length) and continues execution; when done, the DMA controller raises an interrupt.

Pros: high throughput, minimal CPU load. Cons: DMA controller competes with CPU for the memory bus.

Which to choose

  • Slow interactive devices → interrupt-driven.
  • Bulk transfers (disk, network) → DMA.
  • Simple, low-cost embedded systems → programmed I/O.

docs.title: Worked example 6.1 — disk I/O time
docs.text:
Given. Disk with: - Average seek time = 9 ms. - Rotational speed = 7200 RPM (120 rev/s, period 8.33 ms). - Transfer rate = 150 MB/s. - Block size = 4 KB.

Average rotational latency = half a revolution = 4.17 ms.

Transfer time for 4 KB = \(4096 / (150 \times 10^6) \approx 0.027\,\text{ms}\).

Total service time per block ≈ \(9 + 4.17 + 0.027 \approx 13.2\,\text{ms}\).

Random IOPS ≈ \(1 / 0.0132 \approx 76\) IOPS.

For sequential access, seek and rotation are amortised across many blocks — throughput approaches the interface limit.

docs.title: 6.4 Buses
docs.text:
A bus is a set of wires carrying data, addresses, and control signals.

Bus Purpose Typical speed Front-side bus CPU ↔ memory 800 MT/s – 1600 MT/s PCIe Peripheral expansion PCIe 4.0 ×16: ~32 GB/s USB External devices USB 3.2: 20 Gb/s SATA / NVMe Storage SATA 6 Gb/s; NVMe ×4 ~7 GB/s

Modern systems use a point-to-point interconnect (PCIe) rather than a shared bus.

docs.title: 6.5 I/O buffering
docs.text:
Buffering decouples producer and consumer speeds.

  • Single buffering — one buffer; producer fills while consumer drains.
  • Double buffering — two buffers alternate.
  • Circular buffering — ring of buffers for streaming.

Why buffering matters:

  • A CPU produces data far faster than a disk can absorb.
  • A network delivers packets in small chunks, but the file system writes in blocks.
  • Buffering provides a consistent snapshot even if the source changes.

docs.title: 6.6 Quiz
docs.text:
1. Compare programmed, interrupt-driven, and DMA I/O on CPU utilisation and per-transfer overhead.
  2. Compute the average service time for a disk with 10 ms seek, 5400 RPM, and 100 MB/s transfer rate for an 8 KB block.
  3. Why does a modern system use PCIe point-to-point rather than a shared bus?
  4. Explain double buffering with an example.

docs.title: Answer key
docs.text:
Click to reveal
  1. Programmed: high CPU, low complexity. Interrupt: low CPU for slow devices. DMA: minimal CPU, high throughput.
  2. Rotational period = 11.1 ms; half = 5.55 ms. Transfer = 8192/10^8 = 0.08 ms. Total ≈ 10 + 5.55 + 0.08 ≈ 15.6 ms.
  3. PCIe scales better — each device gets its own link, no contention.
  4. Two buffers alternate: while the producer fills one, the consumer drains the other.

docs.title: Chapter 7 — Advanced Topics
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Coverage: parallel processing models (SISD/SIMD/MISD/MIMD) · multicore · GPU computing · low-level data structures · introduction to operating systems.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
1. Classify computer architectures using Flynn's taxonomy.
  2. Describe multicore and GPU architectures and their trade-offs.
  3. Explain how stacks, queues, and linked lists are implemented in hardware-adjacent contexts.
  4. Describe the role of an operating system: process management, memory management, file systems, and scheduling.

docs.title: 7.1 Flynn's taxonomy
docs.text:
Flynn's taxonomy (1966)

Four classes of computer architecture based on the number of instruction streams and data streams:

  • SISD — single instruction, single data — the classic Von Neumann machine.
  • SIMD — single instruction, multiple data — vector processors, GPUs.
  • MISD — multiple instruction, single data — rare, mostly theoretical (systolic arrays).
  • MIMD — multiple instruction, multiple data — multicore CPUs, distributed clusters.
Class Example SISD Single-core Pentium SIMD Intel AVX (256-bit vectors), NVIDIA GPU warp MISD Systolic array in a specialised signal processor MIMD Dual-core ARM Cortex-A, AMD Ryzen, cluster

docs.title: 7.2 Multicore
docs.text:
A multicore processor places two or more CPU cores on a single chip, sharing memory (L3) and I/O.

Implications:

  • Parallel execution of threads requires explicit programming (pthreads, OpenMP, std::thread).
  • Cache coherence — all cores must see a consistent view of memory (MESI, MOESI protocols).
  • Amdahl's law caps the speedup from additional cores.

Modern chips have heterogeneous cores — e.g., ARM big.LITTLE with performance and efficiency cores.

docs.title: 7.3 GPU computing
docs.text:
A GPU is a many-core architecture designed for data-parallel workloads:

  • 1000s of simple SIMT (single instruction, multiple threads) lanes.
  • Large vector processing units.
  • Very high memory bandwidth.
  • Optimised for throughput, not latency.

Programming models:

  • CUDA (NVIDIA)
  • OpenCL (portable)
  • SYCL (Khronos)
  • ROCm (AMD)

When to use a GPU. Problems that:

  • Have abundant data parallelism (same operation on many data items).
  • Are arithmetic-heavy (computation dominates memory traffic).
  • Can amortise kernel launch and data transfer overhead.

Not a fit. Branch-heavy, irregular, or latency-sensitive code.

docs.title: 7.4.1 Stack
docs.text:
Last-in, first-out (LIFO). Implemented with:

  • A pointer to top (SP) and an array in memory.
  • Push: SP ← SP − 4; M[SP] ← value.
  • Pop: value ← M[SP]; SP ← SP + 4.

The stack is used for function calls, local variables, and return addresses.

docs.title: 7.4.2 Queue
docs.text: First-in, first-out (FIFO). Implemented with head and tail pointers, or as a circular buffer.

docs.title: 7.4.3 Linked list
docs.text:
A sequence of nodes; each node has a data field and a next pointer.

  • Insertion at head: O(1).
  • Search: O(n).
  • Memory overhead: one pointer per node.

Linked lists are used in free lists (memory allocators) and page tables (inverted page tables).

docs.title: 7.5 Introduction to operating systems
docs.text:
An operating system is the software layer between applications and hardware. Its main responsibilities:

  • Process management — create, schedule, and terminate processes and threads.
  • Memory management — virtual memory, paging, segmentation.
  • File systems — organise persistent data.
  • I/O management — drivers, buffering, device scheduling.
  • Security — authentication, access control.

Process scheduling algorithms: FCFS, SJF, Round Robin, priority (see the OS course for full treatment).

Virtual memory: the OS uses the TLB and page tables to give each process the illusion of a private address space.

docs.title: 7.6.1 x86 (Intel Core, AMD Zen)
docs.text:
• CISC ISA, variable-length instructions (1–15 bytes).
  • Internally decoded into RISC micro-operations.
  • Deep pipeline (14–20 stages), out-of-order execution, speculative execution.
  • Massive L1/L2/L3 caches.

docs.title: 7.6.2 ARM (Cortex-A series)
docs.text:
• RISC ISA, fixed-length (4 bytes, Thumb 2 bytes).
  • Shallower pipeline than x86 (8–15 stages).
  • Energy-efficient — dominant in mobile.
  • Extensively licensed to SoC vendors (Qualcomm, Apple, MediaTek).

docs.title: 7.7 Quiz
docs.text:
1. Classify the following under Flynn's taxonomy: (a) a four-core CPU; (b) a GPU warp; (c) a single-core Pentium; (d) an NVIDIA tensor core.
  2. Explain why a GPU is good for matrix multiplication but poor for a web server.
  3. Describe a stack-based function call — what is pushed and popped?
  4. Compare x86 and ARM on ISA complexity and energy efficiency.

docs.title: Answer key
docs.text:
Click to reveal
  1. (a) MIMD; (b) SIMD; (c) SISD; (d) SIMD.
  2. Matrix multiplication is massively data-parallel and arithmetic-heavy; a web server has irregular, branch-heavy, latency-sensitive work.
  3. Push return address, saved registers, local variables; pop them on return.
  4. x86 is CISC (complex, high performance); ARM is RISC (simple, energy-efficient).

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Stallings, §17.1–§18.4.
  • Patterson & Hennessy, §6.1–§6.6.
  • Mano, §13.1–§13.4.

docs.title: 1.1 — Organization vs Architecture
docs.text:
Definition (Stallings §1.1)

Computer architecture = attributes visible to a programmer: instruction set, data types, addressing modes, I/O mechanisms.

Computer organization = the operational units and their interconnections that realize the architecture: control signals, memory technology, interfaces.

| Aspect | Architecture | Organization | |---|---|---| | Visible to programmer? | **Yes** | **No** | | Example | Does `MUL` exist? | Is `MUL` a hardware multiplier or repeated add? | | Example | Word size (32 / 64 bits) | SRAM vs. DRAM for main memory | | Example | Number of registers | Physical wiring of the register file | !!! tip "Why the distinction matters" Two CPUs can be **architecturally identical** but **organizationally different** — the same x86 binaries run on Intel and AMD CPUs, but their microarchitectures, power envelopes, and performance profiles differ enormously. Open by anchoring the two words: architecture is the *contract*, organization is the *implementation*. Analogy: architecture is the Java language spec, organization is the JIT compiler. Every subsequent chapter alternates between the two — Chapter 3 is mostly architecture, Chapters 4–5 are mostly organization.

docs.title: 1.2 — Evolution of Computing
docs.text:
The four generations

1st (1945–1955): vacuum tubes, ENIAC, ~5000 additions/s. 2nd (1955–1965): transistors, IBM 7094. 3rd (1965–1980): integrated circuits, IBM System/360, PDP-11. 4th (1980–present): VLSI, PCs, mobile, servers.

!!! abstract "Moore's law" The number of transistors on a chip **doubles approximately every 18–24 months**, and the cost per transistor falls proportionally. ??? warning "Moore's law has slowed since ~2010" - **Power density** (Dennard scaling) broke down — smaller transistors no longer run cooler. - **Manufacturing costs** rise steeply at 7 nm / 5 nm / 3 nm. - **Physical limits** — transistor size and wire delay. The industry's response: shift from **higher clock speed** to **more parallelism** (multicore, GPUs, accelerators).

docs.title: 1.3 — The Von Neumann Bottleneck
docs.text:
Von Neumann model

Instructions and data share the same memory and the same bus between CPU and memory. The CPU cannot fetch an instruction and a data word in the same cycle.

!!! warning "The bottleneck" The bus between CPU and memory is a shared resource. Memory bandwidth — not ALU speed — limits throughput for many workloads. ??? info "The Harvard alternative" **Harvard architecture** separates instruction and data memories, doubling the effective bandwidth. Modern CPUs use a **modified Harvard** design — separate L1 instruction and data caches, unified L2/L3.

docs.title: 1.4 — The Von Neumann Model
docs.text:
┌─────────────┐         ┌──────────────┐
│             │◄───────►│              │
│    CPU      │  Bus    │    Memory    │
│             │◄───────►│              │
└─────┬───────┘         └──────────────┘
      │
┌─────▼───────┐
│  I/O        │
│  Devices    │
└─────────────┘
???+ note "Four components" 1. **CPU** — ALU, control unit, registers. 2. **Memory** — stores both instructions and data. 3. **I/O** — outside-world interface. 4. **Bus** — carries addresses, data, and control signals.

docs.title: 1.5 — The Instruction Cycle
docs.text:
Fetch → Decode → Execute

The CPU repeats three phases for every instruction.

???+ info "**Fetch**" 1. CPU puts the value of the **PC** on the address bus. 2. Memory returns the instruction at that address. 3. CPU loads the instruction into the **IR** and increments the **PC**. ??? info "**Decode**" 1. Control unit reads the **opcode** and determines the instruction type. 2. Source operands are read from the register file. ??? info "**Execute**" 1. ALU performs the operation (or memory access, or branch). 2. Result is written back to a register (or memory). !!! tip "Five stages, five cycles" Modern CPUs split memory access and write-back into separate stages, yielding the **five-stage pipeline** (Chapter 4): IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB.

docs.title: 1.6 — Performance Metrics
docs.text:
The CPU performance equation (Patterson & Hennessy) \[ \text{CPU time} = \text{IC} \times \text{CPI} \times \tau = \frac{\text{IC} \times \text{CPI}}{f} \]

where \(\text{IC}\) = instruction count, \(\text{CPI}\) = cycles per instruction, \(f\) = clock frequency.

??? warning "The three factors are interdependent" - Fewer instructions (CISC-style) → higher CPI. - Higher clock (shorter cycles) → higher CPI (harder pipeline balance). - Optimising one factor often worsens another. ???+ note "**MIPS** — millions of instructions per second" $$ \text{MIPS} = \frac{f}{\text{CPI} \times 10^6} $$ Misleading: ignores instruction complexity. A CISC machine can have higher MIPS but lower throughput than a RISC machine.

docs.title: Worked example 1.1 — CPU time and MIPS
docs.text:
Problem:

Given IC = \(10^8\) instructions, CPI = 2.5, clock = 4 GHz.

???+ note "**Step 1 — CPU time.**" $$ T = \frac{10^8 \times 2.5}{4 \times 10^9} = 0.0625\ \text{s} = \mathbf{62.5\ \text{ms}} $$ ??? info "**Step 2 — MIPS.**" $$ \text{MIPS} = \frac{4 \times 10^9}{2.5 \times 10^6} = \mathbf{1600\ \text{MIPS}} $$ ??? success "**Conclusion.**" The program takes 62.5 ms and the CPU sustains 1600 MIPS — a consistent pair. Walk through the arithmetic. Emphasise that MIPS is derivable from the CPU-time formula — the same information in a different unit. Then ask: if we double the clock and CPI rises to 4, what happens? T stays the same. This motivates Amdahl's law and pipeline awareness.

docs.title: 1.7 — Amdahl's Law
docs.text:
Amdahl's law

If a fraction \(f\) of the execution time is improved by a factor \(s\), the overall speedup is

\[ S = \frac{1}{(1 - f) + \dfrac{f}{s}} \]

As \(s \to \infty\), \(S \to \dfrac{1}{1 - f}\).

!!! warning "The fundamental limit" An optimisation that only touches $10\%$ of the code can give **at most** a $1.11\times$ speedup — regardless of how fast the improvement is. ??? tip "The argument for parallelism" As the serial fraction approaches zero, the potential speedup approaches the processor count. This is why multicore exists: it attacks the **serial bottleneck**.

docs.title: Worked example 1.2 — Amdahl's law
docs.text:
Problem:

A program spends 60% of its time in a routine made 3× faster. Compute the speedup, and the maximum possible speedup.

???+ note "**Step 1 — apply the formula.**" $$ S = \frac{1}{(1 - 0.60) + 0.60/3} = \frac{1}{0.40 + 0.20} = \frac{1}{0.60} \approx \mathbf{1.667} $$ ??? info "**Step 2 — maximum possible speedup.**" Even if the routine became **infinitely fast** ($s \to \infty$): $$ S_{\max} = \frac{1}{1 - 0.60} = \mathbf{2.5} $$ ??? success "**Interpretation.**" The whole program only gets **1.67× faster**, because the other 40% now dominates. No improvement of that routine — no matter how clever — can exceed 2.5×.

docs.title: 1.8 — Benchmarks
docs.text:
Standard benchmark suites
  • SPEC CPU — integer and floating-point.
  • SPECpower — energy efficiency.
  • Geekbench — mobile and desktop.
  • STREAM — memory bandwidth.
  • Linpack — floating-point (TOP500 supercomputer ranking).
??? warning "Benchmarks are imperfect" Vendors can optimise for the benchmark. Real workloads vary enormously. Use benchmarks as a **starting point**, never the whole answer — always test with **your** workload.

docs.title: Chapter 1 — key takeaways
docs.text: **1.** **Architecture** is what the programmer sees; **organization** is how it's built. The same architecture has many organizations.     **2.** **Moore's law** drove 40 years of exponential improvement. It has slowed since ~2010 — the response is **parallelism**, not clock speed.     **3.** The **Von Neumann bottleneck** — a shared bus for instructions and data — is why caches, prefetch, and Harvard-style L1s exist.     **4.** **CPU time = IC × CPI × τ**. The three factors trade off against each other.     **5.** **Amdahl's law** bounds every optimisation by the serial fraction it doesn't touch. The limit is $1/(1-f)$.

docs.title: Next — Chapter 2
docs.text:
Computer Arithmetic.

- Signed number representations: sign-magnitude, 1's complement, 2's complement, biased. - Integer addition and subtraction; overflow detection at the bit level. - Multiplication: shift-add, **Booth's algorithm**. - Division: restoring, non-restoring. - **IEEE-754** floating point: single and double precision, special values, rounding. Every arithmetic operation you will meet inside a CPU is an instance of one of these algorithms — usually with a hardware accelerator.

docs.title: 2.1 — Signed Number Representation
docs.text: Four representations Scheme Bit pattern for \(-x\) Zero? Addition circuit Sign-magnitude flip MSB two zeros (0000, 1000) requires sign handling 1's complement invert all bits two zeros (0000, 1111) end-around carry 2's complement invert + add 1 one zero same adder as unsigned Biased add bias \(B\) one used for exponents !!! tip "Why 2's complement won" - **One zero**. - **Same adder** as unsigned — no separate sign logic. - **Range** for $n$ bits: $[-2^{n-1}, 2^{n-1} - 1]$.

docs.title: Worked example 2.1 — −45 in 8 bits
docs.text:
Problem:

Represent \(-45\) in 8 bits, in all four representations.

???+ note "**Step 1 — positive magnitude.**" $+45 = \texttt{0010 1101}$. ??? info "**Step 2 — sign-magnitude.**" Set the sign bit: `1_010 1101` = $\texttt{1010 1101}$. ??? info "**Step 3 — 1's complement.**" Invert all bits: $\texttt{1101 0010}$. ??? info "**Step 4 — 2's complement.**" Add 1: $\texttt{1101 0011}$. ??? success "**Step 5 — biased (B=127).**" Stored = $127 - 45 = 82$ = $\texttt{0101 0010}$.

docs.title: 2.2 — Integer Addition and Subtraction
docs.text:
2's-complement addition

Add the bit patterns as unsigned integers. Discard the carry out of the MSB. Interpret the result as 2's-complement.

??? abstract "Overflow detection rule" Overflow occurs **iff**: - Both operands are **positive** and the result is **negative**, OR - Both operands are **negative** and the result is **positive**. Formally: $C_{\text{in}} \oplus C_{\text{out}}$ of the MSB. !!! warning "Why the rule works" Overflow means the true mathematical result is outside $[-2^{n-1}, 2^{n-1}-1]$. Two positives adding above $2^{n-1}-1$ wrap to a negative pattern — the bitwise signature of overflow.

docs.title: Worked example 2.2 — Overflow detection
docs.text:
Problem:

Add 0110 (+6) and 0101 (+5) in 4-bit 2's complement.

???+ note "**Step 1 — add as unsigned.**" 
  0110
+ 0101
------
  1011
??? info "**Step 2 — interpret result.**" `1011` has MSB = 1 → negative. 2's complement of `1011` is `0101` = 5. So `1011` = **−5**. ??? warning "**Step 3 — check overflow.**" Both inputs positive; result negative → **overflow**. The true answer is +11, which exceeds the 4-bit 2's-complement range $[-8, +7]$. ??? success "**Conclusion.**" Result = `1011`, overflow = **yes**. In hardware, this triggers the overflow flag (OF).

docs.title: 2.3 — Shift-Add Multiplication
2.4 — Booth's Algorithm
docs.text:
Booth's algorithm (signed)

Examine the current and previous multiplier bit:

\((Q_i, Q_{i-1})\) Action 0 0 no arithmetic 0 1 add multiplicand 1 0 subtract multiplicand 1 1 no arithmetic !!! tip "Why it works" Booth's algorithm rewrites a signed multiplication as a sequence of additions and subtractions. The pair $(Q_i, Q_{i-1})$ detects **transitions** — a string of 1s in the multiplier becomes one subtraction and one addition, saving operations on average. ???+ note "Why it handles signs uniformly" Negative numbers are just 2's-complement bit patterns. The arithmetic shift right **preserves the sign bit**, so negative results propagate correctly.

docs.title: 2.5 — Division
docs.text:
Restoring division
  1. Shift left \(A\) (partial remainder).
  2. Subtract divisor from \(A\).
  3. If \(A < 0\): restore (add divisor back), \(Q_0 = 0\).
  4. Else: \(Q_0 = 1\).
  5. Repeat \(n\) times.
??? note "Non-restoring division" Avoids restore: alternate subtraction and addition based on the sign of $A$. - If $A \geq 0$: $A \leftarrow 2A - M$. - If $A < 0$: $A \leftarrow 2A + M$. At the end, a single restore if $A$ is negative. **Faster** (no restore per iteration) but requires careful sign tracking.

docs.title: 2.6 — IEEE-754 Floating Point
docs.text:
Single precision — 32 bits 
| S | EEEEEEEE | MMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMM |
  1      8                  23

Value = \((-1)^S \times 1.M \times 2^{E - 127}\) (bias 127, hidden leading bit).

??? info "Double precision — 64 bits" 1 sign + 11 exponent (bias 1023) + 52 mantissa. Range ~$10^{308}$, precision ~15–17 decimal digits. ??? warning "Special values" | Exponent | Mantissa | Meaning | |---|---|---| | 0 | 0 | $\pm 0$ | | 0 | $\neq 0$ | Subnormal | | 1–254 | any | Normal | | 255 | 0 | $\pm\infty$ | | 255 | $\neq 0$ | NaN |

docs.title: Worked example 2.4 — Encode 6.75
docs.text:
Problem:

Encode \(6.75\) in IEEE-754 single precision.

???+ note "**Step 1 — binary.**" $6.75 = 110.11 = 1.1011 \times 2^{2}$. ??? info "**Step 2 — sign and exponent.**" Sign = 0. Exponent field = $2 + 127 = 129 = \texttt{1000\,0001}$. ??? info "**Step 3 — mantissa.**" Drop hidden 1, pad to 23 bits: $\texttt{1011\,0000\,0000\,0000\,0000\,000}$. ??? success "**Step 4 — assemble and convert to hex.**" $\texttt{0\,1000\,0001\,1011\,0000\,\ldots} = \mathbf{\texttt{0x40D80000}}$. ??? tip "**Sanity check.**" Decode: exponent = 129 − 127 = 2, mantissa = $1.6875$, value = $1.6875 \times 4 = 6.75$. ✓

docs.title: 2.7 — Floating-Point Arithmetic
docs.text:
Addition algorithm
  1. Align the exponents: shift the smaller operand right until exponents match.
  2. Add mantissas.
  3. Normalise the result.
  4. Round to fit the mantissa.
  5. Check for overflow / underflow.
???+ note "Multiplication algorithm" 1. **Multiply** mantissas. 2. **Add** exponents. 3. **Normalise** and **round**. 4. Sign = XOR of signs. !!! warning "Common pitfalls" - **Floating-point addition is not associative**: `(a+b)+c` may differ from `a+(b+c)`. - **Comparisons with `==` are dangerous** — use a tolerance. - **Catastrophic cancellation**: subtracting nearly equal numbers loses precision. - **Accumulated sums drift** — Kahan summation mitigates.

docs.title: 2.8 — Rounding Modes
docs.text: IEEE-754 rounding modes Mode Behaviour Round to nearest, ties to even Default — least biased Round toward zero Truncate Round toward \(+\infty\) Ceiling Round toward \(-\infty\) Floor   !!! tip "Why ties-to-even?"     Simple "round half up" biases results upward when repeated. Ties-to-even breaks the tie by choosing the neighbour with an even LSB — long-run bias approaches zero.

docs.title: Chapter 2 — key takeaways
docs.text: **1.** **2's complement** is the universal integer representation — one zero, same adder as unsigned, clean overflow detection.     **2.** **Overflow** in 2's complement = both operands same sign, result opposite sign. Can be detected as $C_{\text{in}} \oplus C_{\text{out}}$ of the MSB.     **3.** **Booth's algorithm** handles signed multiplication uniformly — add, subtract, or skip based on the $(Q_i, Q_{i-1})$ pair.     **4.** **IEEE-754** uses sign + biased exponent + hidden-bit mantissa. Single precision: 1 + 8 + 23 bits, bias 127.     **5.** **Floating-point arithmetic is not associative** — numerical code must be written with this in mind.

docs.title: Next — Chapter 3
docs.text:
Instruction Sets and CPU Structure.

- Instruction set taxonomy: stack, accumulator, general-purpose, load-store. - Instruction formats: **R, I, J** (MIPS). - Eight addressing modes. - Register transfer notation (RTN). - Datapath design. - **RISC vs CISC**. Every arithmetic and logic operation from Chapter 2 is exposed to software through **instructions** — Chapter 3 decides what that interface looks like.

docs.title: Chapter 3 — Instruction Sets and CPU Structure
3.1 — Instruction Set Taxonomy
docs.text: Where do operands come from? Class Operands live in... Example Stack top of a pushdown stack Java bytecode Accumulator one special register early 8-bit CPUs General-purpose many named registers x86, ARM, MIPS Register-memory one operand in memory x86 Load-store all operands in registers MIPS, ARM, RISC-V   !!! tip "Load-store is the RISC foundation"     Only `LOAD` and `STORE` touch memory; all ALU operations are register-to-register. Simple to pipeline, simple to optimize.

docs.title: 3.2 — MIPS Instruction Formats
docs.text:
R-type — register-to-register 
| opcode 6 | rs 5 | rt 5 | rd 5 | shamt 5 | funct 6 |

Example: add rd, rs, rt → 000000 rs rt rd 00000 100000.

???+ note "I-type — immediate" 
| opcode 6 | rs 5 | rt 5 | imm16 |
Example: `addi rt, rs, imm`, `lw rt, offset(rs)`, `beq rs, rt, offset`. ???+ note "J-type — jump" 
| opcode 6 | target 26 |
Target = `(PC+4)[31:28] || target << 2` — 28 bits of address from 26-bit field.

docs.title: Worked example 3.1 — Decode 0x012A4020
docs.text:
Problem:

Decode the MIPS instruction 0x012A4020.

???+ note "**Step 1 — binary.**" $\texttt{0000\,0001\,0010\,1010\,0100\,0000\,0010\,0000}$ ??? info "**Step 2 — split fields.**" | Field | Bits | Value | |---|---|---| | opcode | `000000` | R-type | | rs | `01001` | 9 | | rt | `01010` | 10 | | rd | `01000` | 8 | | shamt | `00000` | 0 | | funct | `100000` | `add` | ??? success "**Step 3 — decode.**" $\texttt{add\ \$8,\ \$9,\ \$10}$ — register 8 = register 9 + register 10.

docs.title: 3.3 — Addressing Modes
docs.text: Eight classic modes Mode Effective address (EA) Memory accesses Immediate operand embedded in instruction 0 Register operand in register 0 Direct EA = address field 1 Indirect EA = M[address field] 2 Register indirect EA = R[field] 1 Displacement (base+offset) EA = R[base] + offset 1 Indexed EA = R[index] + address field 1 Relative EA = PC + offset 1   !!! tip "The base+offset workhorse"     Base+offset handles **arrays** (base = array start, offset = index×stride), **structs** (base = struct, offset = field), and **stack frames** (base = frame pointer, offset = local) — all with the same encoding.

docs.title: Worked example 3.2 — Effective addresses
docs.text:
Problem:

Suppose R[5] = 0x1000. Compute the effective address for each mode.

???+ note "**Immediate `lw $t0, 100`**" The value 100 is an immediate, not an address. There is no memory access for the operand itself. ??? info "**Direct (address field 100)**" EA = 100. One memory access. ??? info "**Register indirect `lw $t0, 0($5)`**" EA = R[5] + 0 = 0x1000. One memory access. ??? info "**Base+offset `lw $t0, 8($5)`**" EA = R[5] + 8 = **0x1008**. One memory access. ??? success "**Indirect `lw $t0, @100`**" Read M[100] → gives address A; read M[A] → gives operand. **Two memory accesses.**

docs.title: 3.4 — CPU Registers
docs.text: The essential registers Register Purpose PC Program counter — address of next instruction IR Instruction register — current instruction MAR Memory address register MBR / MDR Memory buffer / data register R0..Rn General-purpose registers SP Stack pointer FLAGS / PSW Condition codes (Z, C, S, V)   !!! tip "PC + IR = the Von Neumann loop"     The **PC** sequences the fetch; the **IR** holds the fetched instruction long enough to be decoded. Without either, there is no instruction cycle.

docs.title: 3.5 — Register Transfer Notation
docs.text:
RTN describes data movement and operations 
MAR ← PC
MBR ← M[MAR]
IR  ← MBR
PC  ← PC + 4
???+ note "Fetch cycle in RTN" 
T0: MAR ← PC
T1: MBR ← M[MAR],  PC ← PC + 4
T2: IR  ← MBR
Three cycles on a **single-bus datapath** — one transfer per cycle. !!! tip "RTN is the bridge between ISA and hardware" Each line of RTN corresponds to one or more control signals. The control unit (Chapter 4) translates the RTN into actual microoperations.

docs.title: 3.6 — Datapath
docs.text: Three datapath designs Design Cycles per instruction Clock period Trade-off Single-cycle 1 Longest path Simple, slow Multi-cycle 3–5 Short Balanced, more control Pipelined ~1 (steady state) Short Fast, complex   !!! warning "The single-cycle cost"     In a single-cycle datapath, every instruction waits for the **slowest** one — usually `LOAD` (memory read). Fast instructions like `ADD` waste most of the cycle.

docs.title: 3.7 — RISC vs CISC
docs.text: The two philosophies Feature RISC CISC Instruction length Fixed Variable Instruction count Few, simple Many, complex Operand sources Registers only Registers or memory Registers Many (32+) Few (8–16) Addressing modes Few Many Control Hardwired Microprogrammed CPI Near 1 2–10 Code size Larger Smaller Pipelining Easy Hard Examples MIPS, ARM, RISC-V x86   ??? info "The RISC argument (1980s)"     Most CISC instructions were **rarely used**; compilers could generate efficient code from a small RISC subset; simple instructions pipeline better; register-only operands are faster.     !!! tip "The modern synthesis"     Modern x86 CPUs decode CISC instructions into **RISC-like micro-operations** internally. Today's RISC/CISC distinction is about the **external ISA**, not the microarchitecture.

docs.title: Chapter 3 — key takeaways
docs.text: **1.** **Load-store** ISAs keep ALU operands in registers — only `LOAD`/`STORE` touch memory.     **2.** **MIPS** has three formats: **R** (register), **I** (immediate), **J** (jump). Decode by splitting the 32-bit word.     **3.** **Base+offset** addressing is the workhorse — it handles arrays, structs, and stack frames with the same encoding.     **4.** **RTN** is the bridge between ISA and hardware: each line corresponds to one or more control signals.     **5.** **RISC** = simple, fixed-length, load-store, easy to pipeline. **CISC** = complex, variable-length, memory operands, microcoded. The boundary is blurred in modern microarchitectures.

docs.title: Next — Chapter 4
docs.text:
Pipelining and Control Unit.

- The five-stage RISC pipeline. - Hazards: structural, data, control. - **Forwarding**, **stalling**, **branch prediction**. - **Hardwired** vs **microprogrammed** control. - **Wilkes'** microcode model. - Horizontal vs vertical microcode. Chapter 3 defined *what* the CPU does; Chapter 4 defines *how* it does it **faster** — by overlapping instructions and centralizing control.

docs.title: 4.1 — Pipeline Concept
docs.text:
Ideal pipeline speedup

A \(k\)-stage pipeline completes one instruction per cycle in steady state. Non-pipelined execution takes \(k\) cycles per instruction.

\[ S_{\text{ideal}} = k \] !!! warning "Realistic speedup" Actual speedup is limited by: - **Hazards** (structural, data, control). - **Fill / drain** time. - **Stage imbalance** — clock period = max stage time. ???+ info "Fill and drain" The first instruction takes $k$ cycles to traverse the pipeline; the last also takes $k$. For a program with $n$ instructions, total cycles $\approx k + (n-1)$. As $n \to \infty$, the overhead vanishes.

docs.title: 4.2 — The Five-Stage RISC Pipeline
docs.text:
IF → ID → EX → MEM → WB Stage Purpose IF Fetch instruction from memory ID Decode, read registers EX ALU operation or address calculation MEM Read/write data memory WB Write result to register ???+ info "Pipeline timing" 
cycle:   1   2   3   4   5   6   7   8
Instr1: IF  ID  EX  MEM WB
