Instr2:     IF  ID  EX  MEM WB
Instr3:         IF  ID  EX  MEM WB
Instr4:             IF  ID  EX  MEM WB
Five instructions overlap in the pipeline simultaneously.

docs.title: 4.3 — Structural Hazards
docs.text:
Definition

Two instructions want the same hardware in the same cycle. Classic case: IF and MEM both need the (single) memory port in a Von Neumann machine.

??? info "The fix" **Split instruction and data memories** (Harvard) — IF reads instruction memory, MEM reads data memory, no conflict. !!! tip "Other structural hazards" - One register-file write port in WB vs. one needed by ID — usually solved by write-then-read design. - Single ALU used by both EX and (some) addressing — solved by a second adder.

docs.title: 4.4 — Data Hazards
docs.text: Three types Type Dependence Meaning RAW read-after-write Consumer needs a value the producer hasn't written yet WAR write-after-read Consumer's read must complete before producer's write (anti-dependence) WAW write-after-write Two writes to the same register (output dependence)   ???+ info "Which need fixing?"     - **RAW** — always present, resolved by **forwarding** and/or **stalling**.     - **WAR**, **WAW** — resolved by **register renaming** in out-of-order CPUs.     ??? warning "Load-use is special"     A `LOAD` produces its value only after the **MEM** stage. The next instruction's **EX** stage starts before that — so even forwarding cannot help. **One stall cycle is required.**

docs.title: 4.5 — Forwarding
docs.text:
Definition

Forwarding (bypass) routes the ALU or memory output directly to a consumer's input, skipping the register file.

???+ info "How it works" 
cycle:    1   2   3   4   5
ADD R1:   IF  ID  EX  MEM WB
SUB R4:       IF  ID  EX  MEM WB
                      ↑
                      EX reads R1 from ADD's ALU output
The value is available at ADD's EX output and needed at SUB's EX input — same cycle, one path. !!! tip "What forwarding does NOT solve" **Load-use** — the load's data is only available after MEM, but the consumer needs it at EX. One stall is unavoidable.

docs.title: Worked example 4.1 — Hazards in ADD/SUB/AND
docs.text:
Problem:

ADD  R1, R2, R3
SUB  R4, R1, R5
AND  R6, R1, R7

Identify all hazards.

???+ note "**Step 1 — dependencies.**" - SUB uses R1 (produced by ADD) → **RAW hazard**. - AND uses R1 (produced by ADD) → **RAW hazard**. ??? info "**Step 2 — stalls without forwarding.**" Each consumer must wait for ADD to reach **WB** (cycle 5): - SUB stalls 2 cycles. - AND stalls 2 cycles. - **Total: 4 stall cycles.** ??? success "**Step 3 — with forwarding.**" - SUB: forward ALU output → **1 stall** (EX→EX not free). - AND: forward MEM/WB output → **0 stalls**. - **Total: 1 stall cycle.**

docs.title: 4.6 — Control Hazards
docs.text:
Definition

The pipeline fetches instructions speculatively, but a branch decides the next PC only in EX (or later). If the branch is taken, the fetched instructions are wrong and must be flushed.

???+ note "Solutions" | Technique | Idea | Cost | |---|---|---| | **Stall** | Wait for resolution | High | | **Predict not-taken** | Continue with fall-through | Low, wrong for taken branches | | **Delayed branch** | Execute 1 instruction from delay slot regardless | One wasted slot | | **Branch prediction** | Static or dynamic prediction | Depends on accuracy | !!! tip "Dynamic prediction" A **branch history table** records the outcome of recent branches. **Two-bit saturating counters** give 90%+ accuracy on typical code — the single biggest win for control-hazard mitigation.

docs.title: Worked example 4.2 — Branch penalty CPI
docs.text:
Problem:

20% branches, 2-cycle misprediction penalty, 90% prediction accuracy, ideal CPI = 1.

???+ note "**Step 1 — misprediction rate per instruction.**" $$ \text{mispredictions} = 0.20 \times 0.10 = 0.02. $$ ??? info "**Step 2 — expected penalty.**" $$ \text{penalty} = 0.02 \times 2 = 0.04\ \text{cycles/instruction}. $$ ??? success "**Conclusion.**" $$ \text{CPI}_{\text{avg}} = 1 + 0.04 = \mathbf{1.04}. $$ The branch cost adds **4%** to the baseline CPI. ??? tip "**Sensitivity.**" If prediction were 100% accurate → CPI = 1. If always wrong → CPI = 1 + 0.20 × 2 = 1.40.

docs.title: 4.7 — Hardwired Control
docs.text:
Definition

The control unit is a finite-state machine — combinational logic generates each control signal from the opcode and current state.

???+ info "Design process" 1. Define the ISA. 2. Draw the state diagram for each instruction type. 3. Derive the truth table (state × opcode → control signals). 4. Minimize with Karnaugh maps or a synthesis tool. 5. Wire up the gates. !!! tip "Pros and cons" **Pros:** Fast — signals appear combinationally, no fetch overhead. **Cons:** Difficult to modify — adding an instruction means redesigning the logic. **Used by:** RISC (MIPS, ARM, RISC-V).

docs.title: 4.8 — Microprogrammed Control
docs.text:
Wilkes' model (1951)

The control unit is a microprogram stored in control memory:

Control Memory (microcode)
      ↓
Microinstruction Register
      ↓
Micro-sequencer (next-address logic)
      ↓
Control signals to datapath

Each machine instruction = a sequence of microinstructions.

???+ info "Horizontal vs vertical microcode" | Aspect | Horizontal | Vertical | |---|---|---| | Encoding | One bit per control signal | Compressed (opcode + operands) | | Width | Wide (100+ bits) | Narrow (20–30 bits) | | Parallelism | Full — all signals in one word | Needs a decoder | | Speed | Fast | Slower | !!! tip "Pros and cons" **Pros:** Flexible — add instructions by appending microcode. Good for complex ISAs. **Cons:** Slower — each instruction needs a sequence of microinstruction fetches. **Used by:** CISC (classic x86, VAX).

docs.title: 4.9 — Hardwired vs Microprogrammed
docs.text: The trade-off Aspect Hardwired Microprogrammed Implementation Complex (FSM) Simpler (microcode) Speed Faster Slower Flexibility Low High Modification Redesign Update microcode Cost Higher design effort Higher control-memory cost Best for RISC CISC Modern use Yes (fast path) Yes (complex instructions)   !!! tip "Modern x86 does both"     Intel/AMD CPUs use **hardwired control for common instructions** and **microcode for rare/complex ones** — a hybrid that captures the best of both.

docs.title: Chapter 4 — key takeaways
docs.text: **1.** A $k$-stage pipeline gives ideal speedup $k$; real speedup is limited by hazards and stage imbalance.     **2.** **Data hazards** (RAW) are the most common; **forwarding** resolves most without stalls, but **load-use** requires one stall cycle.     **3.** **Control hazards** are addressed by **branch prediction**. A 90% accurate predictor adds only ~4% to CPI on typical workloads.     **4.** **Hardwired control** is fast and used in RISC; **microprogrammed** is flexible and used in CISC.     **5.** Modern CPUs are **hybrid**: hardwired for common instructions, microcoded for complex ones.

docs.title: Next — Chapter 5
docs.text:
Memory Systems.

- Memory hierarchy and locality. - SRAM, DRAM, ROM, flash. - Cache organization: direct-mapped, set-associative, fully associative. - Replacement and write policies. - **AMAT** and cache performance. - **Virtual memory** and TLB. - HDD and SSD. The pipeline speedup of Chapter 4 is capped by the **memory wall** — unless the cache hides the 100× gap between registers and DRAM.

docs.title: 5.1 — Memory Hierarchy
docs.text:
Registers          (< 1 KB, < 1 ns)
    ↓
L1 Cache           (32 KB, ~1 ns)
    ↓
L2 Cache           (256 KB, ~5 ns)
    ↓
L3 Cache           (8 MB, ~20 ns)
    ↓
Main Memory (DRAM) (8 GB, ~80 ns)
    ↓
SSD                (256 GB, ~100 µs)
    ↓
HDD                (4 TB, ~10 ms)
???+ note "Why it works — locality" - **Temporal locality** — recently used items are likely to be reused. - **Spatial locality** — items nearby in memory are likely to be used soon. !!! tip "The hierarchy delivers fast-memory speed at cheap-memory cost" A 1% miss rate with a 40 ns miss penalty and 1 ns hit time gives AMAT = 1.4 ns — nearly as fast as pure SRAM, at 1/100 the cost.

docs.title: 5.2 — Memory Technologies
docs.text: SRAM vs DRAM vs flash Type Volatile? Speed Cost Refresh? Typical use SRAM Yes Fastest Expensive No Cache DRAM Yes Medium Cheap Yes (~64 ms) Main memory ROM No Slow Cheap No Firmware Flash No Medium Cheap No SSD, USB HDD No Very slow Very cheap No Bulk storage   ???+ info "Why DRAM needs refresh"     A DRAM cell is **one transistor + one capacitor**. The capacitor leaks charge, so each row must be refreshed every ~64 ms. SRAM uses **flip-flops** — no leakage.

docs.title: 5.3 — Cache Organization
docs.text:
Three organizations Type Placement Pros Cons Direct-mapped one line per block Simple, fast Conflict misses Fully associative any line No conflict misses Expensive (many comparators) Set-associative one set, K ways Good compromise Slightly more complex ???+ info "Address decomposition" For a set-associative cache: 
| Tag | Index | Block offset |
- **Block offset** = $\log_2(\text{block size})$. - **Index** = $\log_2(\text{number of sets})$. - **Tag** = remaining bits.

docs.title: Worked example 5.1 — Cache parameters
docs.text:
Problem:

32 KB cache, 64-byte blocks, 4-way set associative, 32-bit address. Compute blocks, sets, and bit fields.

???+ note "**Step 1 — blocks and sets.**" $$ \text{blocks} = \frac{32\text{KB}}{64\text{B}} = 512, \quad \text{sets} = \frac{512}{4} = 128. $$ ??? info "**Step 2 — bit fields.**" - Index = $\log_2 128 = 7$ bits. - Offset = $\log_2 64 = 6$ bits. - Tag = $32 - 7 - 6 = 19$ bits. ??? success "**Summary.**" | Tag | Index | Offset | |:---:|:---:|:---:| | 19 bits | 7 bits | 6 bits |

docs.title: 5.4 — Replacement Policies
docs.text: Four policies Policy Description When used LRU Evict least-recently used line Best but expensive FIFO Evict oldest line Simple Random Evict a random line Cheap for high associativity Optimal Evict line used furthest in future Theoretical only   !!! warning "LRU is expensive"     Tracking the recency order requires an ordered list per set. Real caches use **pseudo-LRU** (approximate, using a few bits per set) or **random** for high associativity.

docs.title: 5.5 — Write Policies
docs.text: Write-through vs write-back Policy Behaviour Traffic Complexity Write-through Write cache and memory on every store High Simple Write-back Write cache only; update memory on eviction Low Needs dirty bit   ???+ info "Why write-back wins"     Programs that repeatedly write the same line (loops updating an array) would flood memory under write-through. Write-back **amortises** many writes into one — dramatically reducing memory bandwidth.     !!! tip "The cost of write-back"     **Cache coherence** in multicore systems is harder — another core may read stale data from memory if a dirty line hasn't been written back. Modern CPUs use **MESI/MOESI** snooping protocols.

docs.title: 5.6 — AMAT
docs.text: Average memory access time \[ \text{AMAT} = \text{Hit time} + (\text{miss rate} \times \text{miss penalty}) \]   ???+ note "The sensitivity"     Because the **miss penalty** is often 20–100× the hit time, small changes in miss rate have **huge** effect on AMAT.

docs.title: Worked example 5.2 — AMAT
docs.text:
Problem:

Hit time = 2 ns, miss penalty = 40 ns, hit rate 95% and 98%.

???+ note "**Step 1 — 95% hit rate.**" $$ \text{AMAT} = 2 + 0.05 \times 40 = 2 + 2 = \mathbf{4\ \text{ns}}. $$ ??? info "**Step 2 — 98% hit rate.**" $$ \text{AMAT} = 2 + 0.02 \times 40 = 2 + 0.8 = \mathbf{2.8\ \text{ns}}. $$ ??? success "**Interpretation.**" A **3 percentage-point** improvement in hit rate reduces AMAT by **30%**. Cache hit rate dominates memory performance — which is why L1 caches are sized carefully.

docs.title: 5.7 — Virtual Memory
docs.text:
Definition

Virtual memory gives each process its own address space, mapped by the MMU to physical memory. Pages not resident in physical memory are fetched from disk (or SSD) on demand.

???+ note "Paging vs segmentation" | Scheme | Size | Internal frag | External frag | |---|---|---|---| | **Paging** | Fixed (pages/frames) | **Yes** (last page) | **No** | | **Segmentation** | Variable | **No** | **Yes** | !!! tip "The TLB" The **translation lookaside buffer** caches recent page-table entries. With $\alpha \approx 99\%$ hit rate, virtual memory is effectively free — the extra cost is one TLB lookup per access.

docs.title: 5.8 — TLB and AMAT
docs.text:
Effective access time with TLB \[ \text{EAT} = \alpha (t_{\text{TLB}} + t_{\text{mem}}) + (1-\alpha)(t_{\text{TLB}} + 2 t_{\text{mem}}) \]

where \(\alpha\) is the TLB hit rate.

???+ note "Typical numbers" - $t_{\text{TLB}} = 1$ ns, $t_{\text{mem}} = 50$ ns, $\alpha = 0.99$. - $\text{EAT} = 0.99 \times 51 + 0.01 \times 101 = 50.5 + 1.01 = \mathbf{51.5\ \text{ns}}$. TLB miss adds only 1 ns to the 50 ns base — **2%**.

docs.title: 5.9 — HDD vs SSD
docs.text:
HDD — mechanical
  • Platters, heads, tracks, sectors.
  • Seek (~9 ms) + rotation (~4 ms) + transfer (~0.03 ms for 4 KB).
  • Random IOPS ≈ 75–200.
  • Sequential throughput ~100–200 MB/s.
???+ note "SSD — flash" - NAND cells, no moving parts. - **No seek**, **no rotation**. - Random access ≈ **50–100 µs**. - Random IOPS ≈ **100,000+**. - Sequential throughput 500 MB/s – 7 GB/s (NVMe). !!! tip "Why SSDs changed everything" Databases, virtual memory, and filesystems are **random-access** workloads — exactly where HDDs hurt most. SSDs give ~1000× the random IOPS at similar cost-per-byte.

docs.title: Chapter 5 — key takeaways
docs.text: **1.** The memory hierarchy is justified by **locality** — it delivers fast-memory speed at cheap-memory cost.     **2.** Cache **organization** (direct-mapped / set-associative / fully associative) trades simplicity against conflict misses.     **3.** **AMAT** = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty. Hit rate dominates because the miss penalty is 20–100× the hit time.     **4.** **Write-back** reduces memory traffic at the cost of a dirty bit and coherence complexity.     **5.** **Virtual memory** gives every process a private address space; the **TLB** makes it near-free.     **6.** **SSDs** eliminate seek and rotation; random IOPS is 1000× an HDD.

docs.title: Next — Chapter 6
docs.text:
I/O Systems.

- I/O devices and modules. - **Programmed I/O**, **interrupt-driven I/O**, **DMA**. - Buses: PCIe, USB, SATA. - Disk I/O performance. - Buffering. Memory is fast; I/O is slow. Chapter 6 shows how to hide that gap — with DMA, buffering, and interrupt-driven design.

docs.title: 6.1 — I/O Device Classes
docs.text: Three classes Class Examples Transfer unit Access Block HDD, SSD, USB drive Block (512 B – 4 KB) Random Character Keyboard, serial Byte Sequential Network Ethernet, Wi-Fi Packet Streaming   !!! tip "Each class has a natural transfer mechanism"     - Block → **DMA** (large, contiguous).     - Character → **interrupt** (small, unpredictable).     - Network → **DMA + interrupt** (packet-driven).

docs.title: 6.2 — I/O Modules
docs.text:
What is an I/O module?

An I/O controller sits between the bus and the device. It contains: - Data registers — hold the transferred data. - Status register — ready / busy / error. - Control register — start, direction.

???+ info "Two addressing schemes" - **Memory-mapped I/O** — device registers appear at memory addresses; accessed via normal load/store. - **Isolated I/O** — separate address space; dedicated `IN`/`OUT` instructions. !!! tip "Memory-mapped wins in modern systems" Uniform addressing simplifies the ISA and lets the compiler use normal instructions to access device registers.

docs.title: 6.3 — Programmed I/O (Polling)
6.4 — Interrupt-Driven I/O
docs.text:
The algorithm
  1. CPU issues a read command to the device.
  2. Device transfers data in the background.
  3. When ready, the device raises an interrupt.
  4. The CPU enters an interrupt handler, which reads the data.
???+ info "Why it wins" The CPU is **free between transfers** — it can run other processes. For slow devices (keyboard, mouse), the cost per transfer is negligible. ???+ info "Interrupt latency" - Save registers, switch context, run handler, restore — ~100 to 1000 cycles per interrupt. - For **high-frequency** devices (1 Gbps NIC), interrupts would overwhelm the CPU. - Solution: **interrupt coalescing** — batch multiple events into one interrupt.

docs.title: 6.5 — Direct Memory Access (DMA)
docs.text:
The algorithm
  1. CPU programs the DMA controller: source, destination, length, direction.
  2. DMA controller takes ownership of the bus.
  3. Transfers data directly between memory and device.
  4. Raises one interrupt when done.
???+ info "Why it wins" - The CPU does **no per-byte work** — it just configures the transfer once. - Throughput bounded by the bus and DMA controller, not the CPU. - Essential for disks, SSDs, and high-speed networking. ??? warning "The trade-off" The DMA controller **competes with the CPU for the memory bus** — while DMA transfers, the CPU's own memory accesses are slowed (**cycle stealing**). Modern systems minimise this with **direct cache access** and **coherent DMA**.

docs.title: 6.6 — Programmed vs Interrupt vs DMA
docs.text: Comparison Mechanism CPU involvement Per-transfer latency Best for Programmed 100% busy-wait Device speed Simple embedded; very fast devices Interrupt Free between transfers Interrupt overhead Slow interactive devices DMA Minimal (setup only) Setup + DMA time Bulk transfers (disk, network)   !!! tip "Decision rule"     **Slow, rare** → interrupt. **Bulk, frequent** → DMA. **Simple, no interrupt controller** → polling.

docs.title: Worked example 6.1 — Disk I/O time
docs.text:
Problem:

9 ms seek, 7200 RPM, 150 MB/s transfer, 4 KB block.

???+ note "**Step 1 — rotation.**" $T_{\text{rot}} = 60/7200 = 8.33$ ms. Average latency = half = **4.17 ms**. ??? info "**Step 2 — transfer.**" $$ T_{\text{xfer}} = \frac{4096}{150 \times 10^6} \approx 0.027\ \text{ms}. $$ ??? success "**Step 3 — total.**" $$ T_{\text{service}} = 9 + 4.17 + 0.027 \approx \mathbf{13.2\ \text{ms}}. $$ Random IOPS $\approx 1 / 0.0132 \approx \mathbf{76}$.

docs.title: 6.7 — Buses
docs.text: From shared bus to point-to-point Bus Purpose Speed Front-side (obsolete) CPU ↔ memory ~1.6 GT/s PCIe 4.0 ×16 Peripheral expansion ~32 GB/s USB 3.2 External 20 Gb/s SATA 3 Storage 6 Gb/s NVMe ×4 Storage ~7 GB/s   ???+ info "Why PCIe replaced the shared bus"     A **shared bus** forces all devices to arbitrate for the same wires — one slow device blocks all others. **PCIe** is **point-to-point**: each device has its own lane. Bandwidth scales with lane count.

docs.title: 6.8 — Buffering
docs.text:
Definition

Buffering holds data temporarily between producer and consumer to absorb speed mismatches.

???+ note "Three types" - **Single** — one buffer; producer fills while consumer drains. - **Double** — two buffers alternate; producer works while consumer drains. - **Circular** — ring of buffers for streaming. !!! tip "Why buffering matters" - CPU is 1000× faster than disk — without buffering, the CPU would stall on every write. - Network delivers 1500-byte packets, but file systems write 4 KB blocks — buffering aggregates. - Buffering gives a **consistent snapshot** even if the source changes.

docs.title: Chapter 6 — key takeaways
docs.text: **1.** **I/O is 100–1000× slower than the CPU** — the whole I/O subsystem is designed to hide this gap.     **2.** **Programmed I/O** is simple but wastes the CPU; use it only for very fast devices or bare-metal systems.     **3.** **Interrupt-driven I/O** frees the CPU between transfers — the standard for slow interactive devices.     **4.** **DMA** moves data without CPU involvement — essential for bulk transfers (disk, network).     **5.** **PCIe** point-to-point replaced shared-bus architectures — bandwidth scales with lanes.     **6.** **Buffering** absorbs the speed mismatch between producer and consumer.

docs.title: Next — Chapter 7
docs.text:
Advanced Topics.

- **Flynn's taxonomy** (SISD, SIMD, MISD, MIMD). - Multicore processors. - **GPU** computing. - Low-level data structures. - Introduction to operating systems. Chapters 1–6 built a single fast CPU. Chapter 7 asks: what happens when we need **many** CPUs?

docs.title: 7.1 — Flynn's Taxonomy
docs.text:
Flynn's taxonomy (1966)

Four classes based on instruction streams and data streams:

Class Full name Example SISD Single Instruction, Single Data Pentium SIMD Single Instruction, Multiple Data GPU warp, Intel AVX MISD Multiple Instruction, Single Data Systolic arrays (rare) MIMD Multiple Instruction, Multiple Data Multicore CPU, cluster !!! tip "Why Flynn still matters" The classification is 60+ years old but captures the essential design point: does the parallelism come from **many data items** (SIMD) or **many independent tasks** (MIMD)?

docs.title: 7.2 — SIMD
docs.text:
Single Instruction, Multiple Data

One instruction operates on a vector of data items simultaneously. Examples: - Intel SSE / AVX — 128, 256, or 512-bit vector registers. - NVIDIA GPU warp — 32 threads execute the same instruction. - ARM NEON — 128-bit vector extension.

???+ info "When SIMD wins" - **Data parallel** loops — e.g., adding two arrays element by element. - **Arithmetic-heavy** kernels — matrix operations, image processing, cryptography. - **When not to use it**: irregular control flow, branch-heavy code. ???+ note "Speedup" An AVX-512 instruction processes 16 single-precision floats at once — theoretically **16× the throughput** of scalar code, with no change to the algorithm.

docs.title: 7.3 — MIMD and Multicore
docs.text:
Multiple Instruction, Multiple Data

Multiple independent threads, each with its own instruction stream, running on separate cores. The standard model for multicore CPUs, servers, and clusters.

???+ info "Multicore design considerations" - **Cache coherence** — all cores must see a consistent memory view (MESI, MOESI protocols). - **Consistency model** — sequential, total-store-order, or relaxed. - **Interconnect** — shared L3, ring, mesh, crossbar. - **Heterogeneous cores** — ARM big.LITTLE pairs performance with efficiency cores. !!! warning "Amdahl's law caps the speedup" With 10% serial code, a 1000-core CPU gives at most 10× — **not** 1000×. Parallelism helps only when the serial fraction is small.

docs.title: 7.4 — GPU Computing
docs.text:
What is a GPU?

A many-core processor with thousands of simple SIMT lanes (Single Instruction, Multiple Thread). Designed for throughput, not latency.

???+ info "Why GPUs are fast for the right workload" - **Massive parallelism** — thousands of threads. - **High memory bandwidth** (HBM, GDDR6) — 10× a CPU's. - **Latency hidden** by overlapping many independent warps. ???+ note "Programming models" - **CUDA** (NVIDIA) - **OpenCL** (portable) - **SYCL** (Khronos) - **ROCm** (AMD) !!! warning "When NOT to use a GPU" - Branch-heavy, irregular code. - Small data (kernel-launch overhead dominates). - Latency-sensitive (each request has ~microseconds of overhead).

docs.title: Worked example 7.1 — Flynn's taxonomy for four workloads
docs.text:
Problem:

Classify each workload: (a) matrix addition, (b) single-threaded editor, (c) web server, (d) loosely coupled simulation.

???+ note "**(a) Matrix addition → SIMD**" Each element depends only on its counterpart. Identical operation on many data items — pure vectorisation. ??? info "**(b) Text editor → SISD**" Sequential, event-driven, latency-sensitive. Parallelism offers no benefit. ??? info "**(c) Web server → MIMD**" Each request is an independent task on a different core. Multicore and multi-threaded servers fit exactly. ??? info "**(d) Loosely coupled simulation → MIMD**" Sub-tasks are independent, exchange data infrequently. Distributed MIMD (clusters, cloud) suits best. ??? success "**Summary.**" (a) SIMD · (b) SISD · (c) MIMD · (d) MIMD.

docs.title: 7.5 — Low-Level Data Structures
docs.text:
Stack

LIFO. A pointer to the top (SP) plus an array. Push: SP ← SP−4; M[SP] ← value. Pop: value ← M[SP]; SP ← SP+4.

Used for function calls, local variables, and return addresses.

???+ note "Queue" FIFO. Head and tail pointers, or a **circular buffer**. Used in **I/O request queues**, **scheduling**, and **message passing**. ???+ note "Linked list" Sequence of nodes; each node has a data field and a next pointer. - Insert at head: O(1). - Search: O(n). - Memory overhead: one pointer per node. Used in **free lists** (memory allocators) and **page tables**.

docs.title: 7.6 — Introduction to Operating Systems
docs.text:
What an OS does
  • Process management — create, schedule, terminate processes and threads.
  • Memory management — virtual memory, paging, segmentation.
  • File systems — organise persistent data.
  • I/O management — drivers, buffering, scheduling.
  • Security — authentication, access control.
???+ info "Scheduling algorithms" - **FCFS** — first-come, first-served. - **SJF** — shortest job first (optimal for average wait). - **Round Robin** — fixed time quantum. - **Priority** — higher priority runs first (aging avoids starvation). !!! tip "The OS lives on the hardware from Chapters 1–6" Scheduler uses the timer interrupt (Ch 6), virtual memory uses the TLB (Ch 5), context switches save/restore registers (Ch 3), and security uses isolation from protected mode (Ch 1).

docs.title: 7.7 — x86 vs ARM Case Study
docs.text:
x86 — CISC
  • Variable-length instructions (1–15 bytes).
  • Decoded into RISC-like micro-ops internally.
  • Deep pipeline (14–20 stages), out-of-order execution.
  • Massive L1/L2/L3 caches.
  • High performance, high power.
???+ note "ARM — RISC" - Fixed-length (4 bytes, or Thumb 2 bytes). - Shallower pipeline (8–15 stages). - **Energy-efficient** — dominant in mobile. - Licensed to many SoC vendors. !!! tip "The convergence" Modern x86 looks like a RISC machine **inside** — the CISC decoder is just a front end. Modern ARM looks like a wide, out-of-order CPU. The distinction is increasingly about **the ISA contract**, not the microarchitecture.

docs.title: Chapter 7 — key takeaways
docs.text: **1.** **Flynn's taxonomy** captures the essential parallel design choice: SIMD vs MIMD.     **2.** **SIMD** (GPU, AVX) wins on regular, data-parallel workloads with massive throughput.     **3.** **MIMD** (multicore) wins on independent tasks — the standard for servers.     **4.** **GPUs** deliver ~10–100× throughput on the right workloads, but are poor for irregular or latency-sensitive code.     **5.** The **stack**, **queue**, and **linked list** are the primitive data structures that every operating system builds on.     **6.** The **OS** integrates everything from Chapters 1–6 — scheduler on timers, virtual memory on TLB, security on privileged mode.

docs.title: Course wrap-up
docs.text: **The arc of ECEG-3163:**  1. **Chapter 1** — what a computer is, and how to measure it. 2. **Chapter 2** — arithmetic at the bit level. 3. **Chapter 3** — the ISA: what instructions look like. 4. **Chapter 4** — pipelining and control: making it fast. 5. **Chapter 5** — memory: hiding the latency of DRAM. 6. **Chapter 6** — I/O: hiding the latency of devices. 7. **Chapter 7** — advanced: many cores, many threads.     !!! tip "The unifying question"     Every chapter asks: **where is the bottleneck, and what architectural trick hides it?**      - Bottleneck = arithmetic speed → faster ALU, better pipeline.     - Bottleneck = memory latency → caches, virtual memory.     - Bottleneck = I/O latency → DMA, buffering.     - Bottleneck = single-core throughput → more cores, GPUs.

docs.title: A1 — Computer architecture [2]
docs.text:
Answer: (b) — attributes visible to a programmer (instruction set, data types, addressing).

Why the others are wrong.

  • (a) Physical implementation is organization, not architecture.
  • (c) Clock speed is an organizational detail (implementation).
  • (d) The operating system is software built on top of the ISA, not the ISA itself.

Reminder. Architecture = the specification (what a programmer sees). Organization = the implementation (how the hardware realizes it).

docs.title: A2 — Moore's law [2]
docs.text:
Answer: (b) — the number of transistors per chip doubles approximately every 18–24 months.

Why the others are wrong.

  • (a) Clock speed does not double every year; it has plateaued since ~2005 due to power density.
  • (c) Memory latency improves much more slowly than transistor count.
  • (d) Power consumption has been roughly flat since Dennard scaling broke down.

docs.title: A3 — Von Neumann bottleneck [2]
docs.text:
Answer: (b) — the transfer of instructions and data over a single bus.

Why it matters. The CPU cannot fetch an instruction and read/write data simultaneously because both go through the same bus and memory. The Von Neumann bottleneck is why we have caches, prefetching, and split instruction/data L1 caches (Harvard-style).

docs.title: A4 — CPU time and MIPS [3]
docs.text:
Given. IC = \(10^8\), CPI = 2.5, \(f = 4\) GHz \(= 4 \times 10^9\) Hz.

(a) CPU time.

\[ T = \frac{\text{IC} \times \text{CPI}}{f} = \frac{10^8 \times 2.5}{4 \times 10^9} = \frac{2.5 \times 10^8}{4 \times 10^9} = 0.0625\ \text{s} = \mathbf{62.5\ \text{ms}}. \]

(b) MIPS rating.

\[ \text{MIPS} = \frac{f}{\text{CPI} \times 10^6} = \frac{4 \times 10^9}{2.5 \times 10^6} = \mathbf{1600\ \text{MIPS}}. \]

Sanity check. \(1600\) MIPS \(\times\) 62.5 ms \(= 1600 \times 10^6 \times 0.0625 = 10^8\) instructions. ✓

docs.title: A5 — Amdahl's law [3]
docs.text:
Given. \(f = 0.60\) (fraction improved), \(s = 3\) (speedup of the improved part).

\[ S = \frac{1}{(1 - f) + \dfrac{f}{s}} = \frac{1}{(1 - 0.60) + \dfrac{0.60}{3}} = \frac{1}{0.40 + 0.20} = \frac{1}{0.60} \approx \mathbf{1.667}. \]

Interpretation. Even though the routine itself is 3× faster, the whole program is only ~1.67× faster — because the other 40% dominates the new execution time.

Upper bound. Even if the improved part became infinitely fast (\(s \to \infty\)):

\[ S_{\max} = \frac{1}{1 - f} = \frac{1}{0.40} = 2.5. \]

So no optimisation of that routine can exceed a 2.5× speedup of the whole program.

docs.title: B1 — Value of 11110110 in 2's complement [2]
docs.text:
Answer: (a) −10.

Working.

  1. MSB = 1 → negative. Take 2's complement of the remaining bit pattern.
  2. Invert all bits: 00001001.
  3. Add 1: 00001010 = 10.
  4. So the value is −10.

Sanity check. 2's complement of 11110110 should sum to zero with 00001010: 11110110 + 00001010 = 100000000 → carry out, discarded. ✓

docs.title: B2 — IEEE-754 single-precision bias [2]
docs.text:
Answer: (b) 127.

Why the others are wrong.

  • (a) 64 is the bias for the old IBM mainframe short-float format.
  • (c) 128 is a common confusion (it's the number of positive exponents — 1 through 254, i.e. 254 values).
  • (d) 255 is the maximum exponent field (reserved for infinities and NaN).

Range: exponent field \(1\) to \(254\) → unbiased exponent \(-126\) to \(+127\).

docs.title: B3 — Signed multiplication without sign handling [2]
docs.text:
Answer: (b) Booth's algorithm.

Why.

  • (a) Shift-add requires separate sign handling — it multiplies unsigned magnitudes and applies the sign afterward.
  • (b) Booth's algorithm examines adjacent multiplier bits and performs add/subtract/skip operations, so signed and unsigned cases are handled uniformly.
  • (c) and (d) are division algorithms, not multiplication.

docs.title: B4 — −45 in 8-bit [3]
docs.text:
Positive 45 = 00101101.

(a) Sign-magnitude. Set the sign bit to 1, keep magnitude unchanged:

1 0101101

(b) 1's complement. Invert all bits of the sign-magnitude pattern (or equivalently, invert the 8-bit positive form directly):

11010010

(c) 2's complement. Add 1 to the 1's complement:

11010011

Sanity check. Add 11010011 (−45) and 00101101 (+45): 11010011 + 00101101 = 100000000 → carry discarded = 0. ✓

docs.title: B5 — Add 0110 and 0101 in 4-bit 2's complement [3]
docs.text:
Step 1 — add as unsigned.

  0110
+ 0101
------
  1011

Step 2 — interpret result.

1011 has MSB = 1, so it's negative. Take 2's complement: invert = 0100, +1 = 0101 = 5. So 1011 = −5.

Step 3 — overflow check.

  • Operand 1 (0110): MSB = 0 → positive.
  • Operand 2 (0101): MSB = 0 → positive.
  • Result (1011): MSB = 1 → negative.

Rule: if both operands are positive and the result is negative, overflow occurred.

Conclusion. Result = 1011 (= −5), and overflow occurred. The true answer is +11, which exceeds the 4-bit 2's-complement range [−8, +7].

Why it happened. The magnitude 11 is not representable in 4-bit 2's complement — the largest positive value is +7 (0111).

docs.title: B6 — Encode 6.75 in IEEE-754 single precision [3]
docs.text:
Step 1 — binary of 6.75.

  • 6 = 110
  • 0.75 = 0.11 (since 0.5 + 0.25 = 0.75)
  • Combined: 110.11

Step 2 — normalise. Shift the point left by 2:

110.11 = 1.1011 × 2²
  • Mantissa (hidden leading 1): 1.1011
  • Exponent: +2

Step 3 — sign bit. Positive → 0.

Step 4 — exponent field. Add bias 127: \(2 + 127 = 129 = 1000\,0001_2\).

Step 5 — mantissa field. Drop the hidden 1, pad to 23 bits:

1011 0000 0000 0000 0000 000

Step 6 — assemble 32 bits.

S | Exponent  | Mantissa
0 | 10000001  | 10110000000000000000000

Step 7 — hex.

Group into nibbles: 0100 0000 1101 1000 0000 0000 0000 0000

\[ \boxed{\texttt{0x40D80000}} \]

Sanity check. Decode back: exponent = 129 − 127 = 2; mantissa = 1 + 0.1011b = 1.6875; value = 1.6875 × 4 = 6.75. ✓

docs.title: C1 — Base+offset addressing mode [2]
docs.text:
Answer: (c) indexed / base+offset.

Why.

  • Immediate — the operand is encoded inside the instruction itself; no address computation.
  • Direct — the address in the instruction is the effective address; no base register.
  • Register indirect — the effective address is held in a register.
  • Indexed / base+offset — EA = R[base] + offset. This is exactly the wording of the question.

docs.title: C2 — MIPS R-type fields [2]
docs.text:
Answer: (c) opcode, rs, rt, rd, shamt, funct.

MIPS R-type encoding (32 bits):

Field Bits Purpose opcode 6 Always 000000 for R-type rs 5 First source register rt 5 Second source register rd 5 Destination register shamt 5 Shift amount (0 for non-shift) funct 6 Operation selector (e.g. 100000 = add)

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (a) opcode + address is roughly a jump (J-type).
  • (b) opcode, rs, rt, immediate is I-type.
  • (d) opcode + target address — incomplete for J-type (which has 26-bit target).

docs.title: C3 — RISC characteristics [2]
docs.text:
Answer: (b) fixed-length instructions, load-store architecture, many registers.

Why RISC matches (b):

  • Fixed-length instructions decode in a single cycle.
  • Load-store keeps all ALU operands in registers.
  • Many registers reduce memory traffic.
  • Simple addressing modes — designed for pipelining.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (a) Variable-length instructions + microcode are CISC traits (x86).
  • (c) Complex addressing modes are a CISC trait.
  • (d) Microcoded execution is a CISC implementation choice.

docs.title: C4 — Decode 0x012A4020 [4]
docs.text:
Step 1 — binary.

0x012A4020 = 0000 0001 0010 1010 0100 0000 0010 0000

Step 2 — split into R-type fields.

Field Bits Value opcode 000000 R-type rs 01001 9 rt 01010 10 rd 01000 8 shamt 00000 0 funct 100000 add

Step 3 — decode the operation.

  • funct 100000 = add.
  • Opcode 000000 confirms it is an R-type arithmetic/logic instruction.

Step 4 — assembly.

\[ \boxed{\texttt{add\ \$8,\ \$9,\ \$10}} \]

Meaning. $8 = $9 + $10.

docs.title: C5 — Memory accesses per addressing mode [3]
docs.text:
The operand must be fetched. Count memory reads to obtain it:

Mode Effective address Memory reads to fetch operand Why Immediate operand embedded in instruction 0 The operand is already in the IR after fetch. Register operand in a register 0 Read from register file, not memory. Register indirect EA = R[r] 1 One memory read at the address in R[r]. Direct EA = address field 1 One memory read at the address encoded in the instruction. Indirect EA = M[address field] 2 First read fetches the address, second read fetches the operand.

Summary. Immediate and register = 0 memory accesses; register-indirect and direct = 1; indirect = 2.

docs.title: C6 — PC and IR in the instruction cycle [2]
docs.text:
The program counter (PC) stores the address of the next instruction to fetch; it is incremented after each fetch so the CPU knows where to continue. The instruction register (IR) stores the instruction just fetched so the control unit can decode it and generate the correct control signals. Without these two registers, the CPU would have no way to sequence through memory systematically or to hold an instruction long enough to execute it.

In one sentence. The PC sequences the fetch, the IR holds what was fetched — together they realise the Von Neumann fetch-decode-execute loop.

docs.title: Solutions — Chapter 4: Pipelining and Control Unit
docs.text:
Back to Chapter 4

Answers to Section D of the Exam Bank.

docs.title: D1 — Maximum ideal pipeline speedup [2]
docs.text:
Answer: (b) \(k\).

Reason. In an ideal \(k\)-stage pipeline with perfectly balanced stages and no hazards, one instruction completes per cycle after the pipeline fills. Non-pipelined execution takes \(k\) cycles per instruction; pipelined execution takes \(\approx 1\) cycle per instruction in steady state → speedup \(k\).

Caveats. Fill/drain time, hazards, and unbalanced stages reduce the actual speedup below \(k\).

docs.title: D2 — Structural hazard [2]
docs.text:
Answer: (a) two instructions want the same hardware resource.

Examples. IF and MEM both needing the single memory port in a Von Neumann datapath; two instructions wanting to write to the register file in the same cycle.

Why the others are wrong.

  • (b) Two instructions with a data dependence = data hazard.
  • (c) A taken branch = control hazard.
  • (d) A page fault = a memory-management event, not a pipeline hazard.

docs.title: D3 — Branch prediction addresses [2]
docs.text:
Answer: (c) control hazards.

Why. Control hazards occur when the pipeline does not know which instruction to fetch next (fall-through vs branch target). Branch prediction guesses the outcome so the pipeline can keep fetching without stalling; on a correct prediction there is no penalty, on a misprediction the pipeline flushes and refetches.

docs.title: D4 — Data hazards in ADD/SUB/AND sequence [4]
docs.text:
Sequence.

ADD  R1, R2, R3
SUB  R4, R1, R5
AND  R6, R1, R7

Step 1 — identify hazards.

  • SUB uses R1, produced by ADD → RAW hazard.
  • AND uses R1, produced by ADD → RAW hazard.

(No WAR or WAW hazards here because ADD writes R1 first and both SUB/AND only read it.)

Step 2 — stalls without forwarding.

Without forwarding, an instruction must wait until the producer has written the register in WB before its consumer can read it in ID.

  • ADD writes R1 at end of its WB (cycle 5 if fetched at cycle 1).
  • SUB would need R1 in ID (cycle 3); it must wait until cycle 5 → 2 stall cycles.
  • AND likewise must wait until cycle 5 for R1 → 2 stall cycles.

Total: 4 stall cycles.

Step 3 — how forwarding resolves each hazard.

  • SUB: forwarding from ADD's EX output directly to SUB's EX input reduces the stall to 1 cycle (or 0 if the datapath allows EX→EX forwarding in the same cycle). Standard MIPS implementations use 1.
  • AND: by the time AND reaches EX, ADD's result has been available for two cycles; the value is forwarded from MEM/WB, and no stall is needed.

Total with forwarding: 1 stall cycle.

docs.title: D5 — Hardwired vs microprogrammed control [4]
docs.text:
Step 1 — implementation complexity.

  • Hardwired: combinational logic (FSM). Design is more complex because every control signal must be hand-derived from the truth table. Difficult to modify — adding an instruction requires redesign.
  • Microprogrammed: control memory (ROM) holding a sequence of microinstructions. Design is simpler; adding an instruction means appending a microprogram.

Step 2 — speed.

  • Hardwired: faster. Control signals are combinational — no microinstruction fetch.
  • Microprogrammed: slower. Each instruction requires a sequence of microinstruction fetches (like a tiny program).

Step 3 — flexibility.

  • Hardwired: less flexible. Any change means new silicon (or a major revision).
  • Microprogrammed: more flexible. Update the microcode to fix bugs or add instructions.

Step 4 — architecture class.

  • RISC (MIPS, ARM, RISC-V) typically uses hardwired control — the small, regular ISA suits it.
  • CISC (classic x86, VAX) typically uses microprogrammed control — the complex ISA needs the flexibility.

Bonus. Modern x86 has both: a hardwired fast path for common instructions plus a microcode engine for complex ones.

docs.title: D6 — Average CPI with branch penalty [4]
docs.text:
Given.

  • Branch frequency = \(20\%\).
  • Prediction accuracy = \(90\%\).
  • Taken-branch penalty = 2 cycles.
  • Ideal CPI = 1.

Step 1 — compute the misprediction rate per instruction.

Only 20% of instructions are branches; of those, 10% are mispredicted:

\[ \text{Misprediction rate per instruction} = 0.20 \times 0.10 = 0.02. \]

Step 2 — add the expected penalty.

\[ \text{CPI}_{\text{avg}} = \text{Ideal CPI} + (\text{misprediction rate per instruction}) \times (\text{penalty}) \] \[ = 1 + 0.02 \times 2 = 1 + 0.04 = \mathbf{1.04}. \]

Interpretation. Every instruction takes, on average, \(1.04\) cycles. The branch cost adds 4% to the baseline CPI.

If prediction accuracy were 100%. \(\text{CPI} = 1\) — no penalty. If prediction were always wrong. \(\text{CPI} = 1 + 0.20 \times 2 = 1.40\).

docs.title: Solutions — Chapter 5: Memory Systems
docs.text:
Back to Chapter 5

Answers to Section E of the Exam Bank.

docs.title: E1 — Justification for memory hierarchy [2]
docs.text:
Answer: (c) locality of reference.

Why. Both temporal and spatial locality mean that the data used by a program is clustered in time and space. This clustering is what allows a small, fast top of the hierarchy to serve most accesses, delivering the average performance of a fast memory at the cost of a cheap memory.

docs.title: E2 — DRAM refresh [2]
docs.text:
Answer: (b) it stores each bit as charge on a capacitor that leaks.

Why. A DRAM cell is one transistor plus one capacitor. The capacitor holds charge that represents the bit, but leakage drains it. Each row must be refreshed every ~64 ms or the bits are lost.

Why the others are wrong.

  • (a) DRAM does not use flip-flops — SRAM does.
  • (c) Speed is not the reason for refresh.
  • (d) Volatility is a consequence of the same physics, not the mechanism.

docs.title: E3 — Direct-mapped set selection [2]
docs.text:
Answer: (c) the index bits.

Why. A direct-mapped cache has exactly one allowed line per block:

\[ \text{line} = \text{block}\bmod N, \]

where \(N\) is the number of lines. The block offset selects the byte; the tag confirms a hit; the index (bits between offset and tag) selects the line.

docs.title: E4 — Write-back advantage [2]
docs.text:
Answer: (b) writes accumulate in the cache and reach memory only when the block is evicted.

Why. With write-back, each write updates the cache line (and sets a dirty bit); the memory is only updated when the dirty line is evicted. For programs that repeatedly update the same line, this amortises many memory writes into one.

Why the others are wrong.

  • (a) Every write going to memory is exactly write-through.
  • (c) Both policies cache reads.
  • (d) Block size is independent of the write policy.

docs.title: E5 — Cache parameters [4]
docs.text:
Given. 32 KB total, 64-byte blocks, 4-way set associative, 32-bit address.

Step 1 — number of blocks.

\[ \text{Blocks} = \frac{32 \text{ KB}}{64 \text{ B}} = \frac{32 \times 1024}{64} = \frac{32768}{64} = 512. \]

Step 2 — number of sets.

With 4-way associativity, each set holds 4 lines:

\[ \text{Sets} = \frac{512}{4} = 128. \]

Step 3 — index bits.

\[ \text{Index bits} = \log_2 128 = 7. \]

Step 4 — block-offset bits.

\[ \text{Offset bits} = \log_2 64 = 6. \]

Step 5 — tag bits.

\[ \text{Tag bits} = 32 - (\text{index} + \text{offset}) = 32 - 7 - 6 = \mathbf{19}. \]

Summary table.

Component Bits Count Tag 19 — Index 7 128 sets Block offset 6 64 B blocks Total 32

docs.title: E6 — AMAT at two hit rates [4]
docs.text:
Formula.

\[ \text{AMAT} = \text{Hit time} + (\text{Miss rate} \times \text{Miss penalty}) \]

Case 1 — 95% hit rate.

  • Hit time = 2 ns
  • Miss rate = 0.05
  • Miss penalty = 40 ns
\[ \text{AMAT}_{0.95} = 2 + 0.05 \times 40 = 2 + 2 = \mathbf{4\ \text{ns}}. \]

Case 2 — 98% hit rate.

  • Miss rate = 0.02
\[ \text{AMAT}_{0.98} = 2 + 0.02 \times 40 = 2 + 0.8 = \mathbf{2.8\ \text{ns}}. \]

Interpretation. A 3 percentage-point improvement in hit rate reduces AMAT by 30% (from 4.0 ns to 2.8 ns). This is why cache hit rate dominates memory performance — the miss penalty is so large that small changes in hit rate produce large changes in AMAT.

docs.title: E7 — Paging vs segmentation [4]
docs.text:
Step 1 — paging.

  • Fixed-size pages (logical) and frames (physical), e.g. 4 KB.
  • Any page fits in any frame → no external fragmentation.
  • The last page of a process may be partially filled → internal fragmentation up to page size − 1.

Step 2 — segmentation.

  • Variable-size logical segments (code, data, stack).
  • Segments are allocated with exact size → no internal fragmentation.
  • Free memory between segments is scattered in variable-size holes → external fragmentation.

Step 3 — summary.

Scheme Internal frag External frag Paging Yes (last page) No Segmentation No Yes

Modern systems use segmentation with paging — each segment is paged, combining logical structure with fragmentation-free allocation.

docs.title: E8 — SSD has no seek time [2]
docs.text:
An SSD stores data in NAND flash cells with no moving parts — there is no head to move and no platter to rotate. Therefore:

  • Seek time = 0 (no head movement).
  • Rotational latency = 0 (no rotation).

The access time is determined purely by the flash-controller latency and bus transfer, typically ~50–100 µs for reads.

Effect on random vs sequential.

  • HDD: random reads are dominated by seek + rotation (~10 ms), so random is ~100× slower than sequential (which amortises seek across the transfer).
  • SSD: random reads cost almost the same as sequential reads at the block level; throughput for random may still be somewhat lower due to smaller per-request transfer, but there is no order-of-magnitude penalty.

This is why databases, filesystems, and virtual-memory swap became dramatically faster when SSDs replaced HDDs — random-access workloads are exactly where the HDD's mechanics hurt most.

docs.title: Solutions — Chapter 6: I/O Systems
docs.text:
Back to Chapter 6

Answers to Section F of the Exam Bank.

docs.title: F1 — Programmed I/O [2]
docs.text:
Answer: (c) continuously polls the device status register.

Why. In programmed I/O, the CPU issues a request then busy-waits in a loop, checking the device's ready status. No interrupt is generated; the CPU does all the work.

Why the others are wrong.

  • (a) Being interrupted is interrupt-driven I/O.
  • (b) DMA is a distinct transfer mechanism.
  • (d) An I/O processor is a separate unit, not part of the CPU.

docs.title: F2 — DMA reduces CPU load [2]
docs.text:
Answer: (b) the DMA controller transfers data between memory and device without CPU intervention.

Why. Once the CPU configures the DMA controller (source address, destination, length, direction) and starts the transfer, the DMA controller takes ownership of the bus and moves data directly. The CPU resumes executing other instructions and receives a single interrupt when the transfer finishes.

Why the others are wrong.

  • (a) The CPU is not slower; the point is to free it from an active role.
  • (c) Fewer interrupts is a consequence, not the mechanism.
  • (d) Whole-sector transfers are a property of the device, not of DMA.

docs.title: F3 — Programmed vs interrupt vs DMA [4]
docs.text:
Step 1 — CPU involvement.

  • Programmed: 100% CPU — the CPU busy-waits, checking the status register in a tight loop until data is ready.
  • Interrupt-driven: CPU is free between transfers; the device raises an interrupt per completed transfer. Per-transfer CPU overhead is moderate.
  • DMA: minimal CPU involvement. The CPU sets up the transfer once and can do other work.

Step 2 — latency per transfer.

  • Programmed: latency equals the wait time (potentially long for slow devices). The CPU is blocked.
  • Interrupt-driven: latency is the interrupt-handling time plus the wait. Better than programmed, but per-transfer.
  • DMA: latency is the setup time plus the DMA transfer time. Highest per-setup latency, but throughput dominates for bulk transfers.

Step 3 — suitability.

Device class Programmed Interrupt DMA Slow interactive (keyboard) Poor Best Poor Medium-speed (network) Poor Good Best High-speed bulk (disk, SSD) Terrible Bad Best Simple embedded Best Okay Not available

Rule of thumb. Slow devices → interrupt. Bulk devices → DMA. Simple, low-cost systems → programmed polling.

docs.title: F4 — Disk service time [4]
docs.text:
Given.

  • Average seek time = 9 ms
  • Rotational speed = 7200 RPM
  • Transfer rate = 150 MB/s
  • Block size = 4 KB

Step 1 — average rotational latency.

One revolution takes

\[ T_{\text{rot}} = \frac{60\ \text{s}}{7200\ \text{RPM}} = 8.333\ \text{ms}. \]

Average rotational latency = half a revolution:

\[ \overline{L_{\text{rot}}} = \frac{T_{\text{rot}}}{2} = \frac{8.333}{2} = \mathbf{4.17\ \text{ms}}. \]

Step 2 — transfer time for 4 KB.

\[ T_{\text{transfer}} = \frac{4096}{150 \times 10^6}\ \text{s} \approx 2.73 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{s} \approx \mathbf{0.027\ \text{ms}}. \]

Step 3 — total average service time.

\[ T_{\text{service}} = \text{seek} + \text{rotation} + \text{transfer} = 9 + 4.17 + 0.027 \approx \mathbf{13.2\ \text{ms}}. \]

Sanity check — IOPS.

\[ \text{IOPS} = \frac{1}{0.0132\ \text{s}} \approx 76. \]

So a typical 7200-RPM HDD delivers ~75–80 random IOPS. An SSD delivers ~100,000+ random IOPS on the same workload — a factor of ~1000× improvement, exactly the difference that made SSDs transformative for database and VM workloads.

docs.title: Solutions — Chapter 7: Advanced Topics
docs.text:
Back to Chapter 7

Answers to Section G of the Exam Bank.

docs.title: G1 — SIMD [2]
docs.text:
Answer: (b) one instruction on multiple data items.

Why. In SIMD, a single instruction operates on a vector of data — e.g., one VADDPS instruction adds 8 floating-point numbers to another 8 simultaneously. Examples: Intel SSE/AVX vector instructions, NVIDIA GPU warps executing one instruction per lane, systolic arrays.

Why the others are wrong.

  • (a) SISD is the classic Von Neumann single instruction, single data.
  • (c) MISD is multiple instructions on the same data — very rare.
  • (d) MIMD is multiple independent threads, each with its own instruction stream (multicore CPUs).

docs.title: G2 — GPU throughput [2]
docs.text:
Answer: (b) uses thousands of simple cores to execute many threads in parallel.

Why. A GPU prioritises throughput over single-thread latency: each core is simple and many are placed on the die. Hundreds of threads are scheduled per cycle, hiding memory latency by overlapping many independent requests.

Why the others are wrong.

  • (a) GPUs typically run at lower clock speeds than CPUs.
  • (c) GPU caches are small; the throughput win comes from parallelism, not caching.
  • (d) GPU memory (GDDR, HBM) is high bandwidth but higher latency than CPU DRAM — again, throughput, not latency.

docs.title: G3 — Flynn's taxonomy for four workloads [4]
docs.text:
Workload (a) — Element-wise matrix addition.

  • Best class: SIMD.
  • Why: each output element depends only on the corresponding input elements, with identical operations. Perfectly data-parallel — vectorises trivially or runs on a GPU at huge speedup.

Workload (b) — Single-threaded text editor.

  • Best class: SISD.
  • Why: the workload is sequential, event-driven, and latency-sensitive. Parallelism offers no benefit — the user waits on the UI, not on computation.

Workload (c) — Web server handling 10,000 simultaneous clients.

  • Best class: MIMD.
  • Why: each request is an independent task, executed on a different core (or a different server). Multicore CPUs and multi-threaded servers fit the MIMD model exactly.

Workload (d) — Scientific simulation with loosely coupled sub-tasks.

  • Best class: MIMD.
  • Why: sub-tasks are independent, may take variable time, and exchange data infrequently. Distributed MIMD (clusters, cloud) suits it best. If the sub-tasks were tightly coupled and regular, SIMD or a GPU would also fit — but "loosely coupled" points to MIMD.

Summary.

Workload Flynn class (a) Matrix addition SIMD (b) Text editor SISD (c) Web server MIMD (d) Simulation MIMD
